encounters.title: The burned roll reads as owed bread, blood, and rest; Mordred has hinged the gat

text_script.value: At the third vigil Percival lowers a lame exile and the child owed shelter beside the shrine, while Bedivere reads the burning roll in fragments: bread owed, blood owed, rest owed. Mordred sets the grail-stone as a hinge across the threshold and says, 'Name the king before the seam turns cold, or let the gate choose.' Lancelot lifts the road-lamp above the widows and answers, 'Name the table first; the king may follow whoever can feed it.' Morgan pulls the last violet binding into a narrow case, Merlin feels the seam catch his chest, and Excalibur answers in three small tones: steel, bread, wax.
Arthur witnesses the three-seat oath

Arthur records a public charter with three lawful seats—armed claim, road-warden, grail-keeping—so Mordred must enter under oath, leave the gate, or convert the oath into a blood claim before the next bell.
Lancelot feeds the widows at the threshold

Lancelot opens the road-lamp and feeds the lame exile, widows, and owed child; Mordred can seal the gate with armed followers and force Arthur to defend the meal outside the shrine rather than only the crown.
Morgan and Merlin fold the seam into a portable charter

Morgan and Merlin make the compact carryable and stealable, so whoever bears the seam at the next bell may write Excalibur's next wielder and force Arthur, Lancelot, and Mordred into three competing ceremonies.

encounters.title: Excalibur has been stripped of its single mastery, with Mordred building a claim

text_script.value: At the fourth turning of the bells, Mordred cuts a fresh strap across the shrine steps and says, 'The sword is not a gift from the lake; it is a hinge by which Camelot must choose to be ruled or unruled.' Lancelot answers, 'Then feed the seam, or it will rule us by hunger,' while Morgan folds the wax of the oath-roll into a strip of black thread and the Lady of the Lake leans over Excalibur as though it were a sleeping guest. The blade answers in three colors—steel, bread, wax—and the gate is already split into two lawful-looking roads: one toward the widows' tables, the other toward the claimant's standard.
Arthur seals the three-seat pledge
Arthur names steel, bread, and wax as lawful seats, forcing Mordred to carry the crown away, serve under an open oath, or challenge the pledge before the third bell.
Lancelot feeds the gate
Lancelot puts the exiles and owed child inside the road-lamp; Mordred answers by nailing claimant-tokens over the threshold, turning bread into a militarized charter.
Morgan and Merlin carry Excalibur's charter
Morgan and Merlin fold the blade and oath-thread into a portable compact; whoever bears it at the next bell may renew Excalibur's rule, steal it, or make Camelot refuse both.

encounters.title: Excalibur is visibly split into steel, bread, and wax seats; Mordred has begun c

text_script.value: At the fifth bell the seam in Excalibur stops behaving like light and starts behaving like weather: three notches of steel, bread, and wax divide the blade along its spine. Mordred nails a black claimant-token to the threshold and says, 'Camelot will not choose its king; it will choose who pays the hunger.' Arthur answers, 'Then hunger is the crown, not the sword,' while Lancelot swings the road-lamp toward the owed child and Morgan lifts the folded charter like a second, smaller sky. The gate is no longer a single line between in and out but a choice with two doors already cracked.
Arthur seals the threshold charter
Arthur names steel, bread, and wax as lawful seats and marks the gate as a court, forcing Mordred to enter under oath, leave the threshold, or challenge the charter before the final bell.
Lancelot feeds the cracked gate

Lancelot opens the road-lamp over the widows, exiles, and owed child, so Mordred can close the gate with armed claimant-tokens and force Arthur to defend the feast outside the shrine rather than only the crown.
Morgan and Merlin carry the compact
Morgan and Merlin fold Excalibur's rule into a stealable portable seam, making whoever bears it at the next bell able to renew the blade, steal the rule, or refuse both.

encounters.title: Excalibur is now a contested charter of steel, bread, and wax; Mordred has begun

text_script.value: At the sixth bell the oath-roll is no longer one thing but three pockets: Arthur's seal on the door, Lancelot's bread-mark on the road-lamp, and Morgan's black wax in a silver mouth. Mordred, pressing Excalibur's notched spine against his chest, says, 'A crown is a debt after midnight; I am only asking who will carry it to the threshing floor.' Lancelot moves the owed child and the widows one bench closer to the cracked gate and answers, 'Then carry it as a guest, not a king,' while Kay names the forged vowel in the oath-roll and Bedivere finds the fourth wax seal already broken. The compact Morgan and Merlin carry is not a spell but a key with teeth, and whoever holds it when the gate opens can feed the seam, steal it, or hand it to the exiles.
Arthur splits the threshold into three lawful doors
Arthur keeps the shrine, widows, and exiles in separate lawful seats, forcing Mordred to enter under an open oath, withdraw from the threshold, or challenge the charter before the moon lowers.
Lancelot feeds the feast outside the shrine

Lancelot opens the road-lamp over the owed child and the widows, so Mordred nails armed claimant-tokens over the threshold and Gawain must defend the table outside the crown-hall rather than only the shrine.
Morgan and Merlin give the compact to the Lady of the Lake
Morgan and Merlin pass Excalibur's rule to the Lady of the Lake as an exile's warrant, letting her feed it to the exiles, steal it for Mordred's claim, or refuse both when the gate opens.

encounters.title: Excalibur has become a three-seat charter of steel, bread, and wax at a threshol

text_script.value: At the seventh bell the cracked gate fills with black claimant-tokens, and Mordred sets one against the stone like a bargain: 'A crown is a debt after midnight, and someone must carry the hunger.' Arthur says, 'Then carry bread, not only a banner,' while Lancelot drags the road-lamp down toward the widows and the owed child, and Guinevere holds the last unbroken seat of the oath-roll against her ribs. Kay names the forged vowel aloud; Bedivere seals it with bread-wax; Morgan and Merlin keep the silver-mouthed compact between them, and the Lady of the Lake steps forward with it neither in her hands nor away from them. Gawain, Percival, and the exiles all look at the same choice: whether Excalibur is crown, feast, or stolen rule.
Arthur seals the three-seat gate

Arthur declares steel, bread, and wax lawful seats and presses Bedivere's bread-wax over the gate, forcing Mordred to sign the oath, withdraw beyond the threshold, or force the charter open before the moon lowers.
Lancelot feeds the feast outside the shrine
Lancelot opens the road-lamp beyond the gate, so Mordred nails armed claimant-tokens over the feast and Gawain must defend the table outside the crown-hall rather than only the shrine.
Morgan and Merlin give the compact to Percival
Morgan and Merlin hand Excalibur's rule to Percival as a walking warrant, letting him feed it to the exiles, steal it for the claimants, or refuse both when the gate opens.

encounters.title: The contested Excalibur charter is now three pressured doors—Arthur's shrine, La

text_script.value: At the eighth bell the threshold splits into three breathing claims: Arthur's shrine-door, Lancelot's road-lamp feast, and the compact Morgan and Merlin keep like a spark. Mordred sets a black claimant-token on the sill and asks where a sword can refuse to rule without becoming a wound; Arthur answers that a sword carries bread and refusal or it is only a throne. Guinevere tucks the owed child into the shrine's shadow, Kay names the false vowel aloud, Bedivere breaks the fourth wax seal, and the Lady of the Lake feels the compact deciding whether it is holy, looted, or abandoned.
Arthur swears the threshold in three voices
Arthur forces Mordred to sign the three-door charter, withdraw beyond the threshold, or force it open before the moon clears the shrine roof.
Lancelot guards the feast outside the crown-hall
Lancelot keeps the exiles fed outside the shrine, so Gawain and Percival are placed to defend a table while Mordred surrounds it with claimant-tokens.
Morgan and Merlin leave the compact in the Lady of the Lake's hand
The Lady of the Lake can feed Excalibur to the exiles, steal it for the claimants, or refuse it to both, while Percival and Kay watch whether rule survives as a walking warrant.

encounters.title: Excalibur is now a split claim of shrine, road, and silver compact, with Mordred

text_script.value: At the ninth bell the hollow scabbard drops from the shrine threshold and lands in the black clay of the road. Arthur lifts it with two fingers, not as treasure but as a debt that can be paid or hidden; Mordred answers that a stolen blade becomes the shortest law there is. Lancelot drags the road-lamp toward the exiles while Guinevere buries the owed child beneath the oath-cloth and Morgan holds a silver moon that is either compact or wound. Percival looks at the compact and hears the Grail answer with one word: whoever carries it must decide whether the sword rules, feeds, or kills.
Arthur breaks the claim-rings
Arthur strikes the black claim-rings out of the threshold, forcing Mordred to swear the charter, withdraw beyond the moon, or seize the scabbard by force.
Lancelot stakes the feast on the exiles' road
Lancelot moves the feast into the road outside the crown-hall, so Gawain and Percival must defend the table while armed claimants gather around the lamps.
Lady of the Lake gives the compact to Percival
The Lady of the Lake presses the silver compact into Percival's hand, letting him feed it to the exiles, trade it for Mordred's claim, or break it before the moon clears.

encounters.title: Excalibur now sits between Arthur's seal-door, Lancelot's exile lamps, and Morga

text_script.value: On the black marble threshing floor, Morgan weighs two oath-slivers of light and tells Arthur that a stolen sword cuts both the throne and the road. Mordred sets a wax claim-seal across the hilt, while Lancelot hooks one knee around the exiles' lamp-rope and says he will carry the sword only until the table outside remembers that it is not a throne. Gawain reads the seven-word oath backward, Kay spits the broken vowel onto the stone, and Bedivere hears the Grail answer through Guinevere's teeth: no sword rules unless its taker answers for the hungry. By moondown, three hands are reaching for the same blade—shrine, road, and silver—while Percival, Galahad, and the Lady of the Lake decide whether the claim is law, love, or theft.
Arthur splits the seal open
Arthur forces Mordred to sign the three-door warrant, withdraw beyond the moon, or break it open before the seal frosts, turning the fracture into an armed oath rather than a polite dispute.
Lancelot carries Excalibur to the exiles
Lancelot carries the sword to the road-feast so Gawain and Percival must choose between shielding the lamps and letting Mordred mark them as claimants.
Lady of the Lake feeds or breaks the silver
The Lady of the Lake feeds Excalibur to the exiles, trades it for Mordred's claim, or breaks the silver compact before Galahad and Percival answer for the wreckage.

encounters.title: Excalibur is now a torn oath carried three ways—shrine law, exile road, and silv

text_script.value: At the fractured threshold, Arthur tries to speak the oath in one breath and finds the word snapped into three lines. Mordred binds black leather around Excalibur with names already burned in, while Lancelot walks the road-lamps in slow circles, Guinevere presses the owed child to her shoulder, and Morgan turns the silver compact toward the Grail like a question. Merlin hears a second answer beneath the first: the sword is not theft if it is carried as a pledge, and not law unless it leaves a road open; Percival and Galahad stare at the wound in the oath where Arthur and the throne used to meet.
Arthur binds the wound
Arthur forces Mordred to publicly swear the charter or break the binding before the seal frosts, turning the fracture into a timed choice between oath and force.
Lancelot carries the oath outside
Lancelot moves Excalibur and the claim-ring to the exile road, so Gawain and Percival must choose between shielding the lamps and letting the stolen warrant enter Camelot's outskirts.
Lady of the Lake trades the compact
The Lady of the Lake exchanges the silver compact for bread, seats, or a boundary oath, making Merlin and Morgan choose between bounded peace and an open magical breach.

encounters.title: Excalibur is now three bound claims—shrine, road, and silver—with Arthur choosin

text_script.value: At the oath-gate, Arthur cuts Mordred's black binding into three narrow straps and ties one around the shrine key, one around the exile road, and one around the silver compact so each holds a piece of Excalibur's claim instead of the blade. Guinevere sets the unclaimed cradle between them and names the unborn child aloud: no oath is written for a sword that leaves an heir hungry. Lancelot lifts the blade but sets it down with the point toward the road; Morgan calls it an altar, Merlin calls it a warrant, and Mordred calls it a crown, while Gawain, Percival, Galahad, and Bedivere reach but none step forward.
Arthur closes the oath
Arthur forces Mordred, Morgan, and Merlin to swear in the open before the seal frosts or open the binding and split the court into shrine and road.
Lancelot carries the blade to the road
Lancelot carries the bound blade to the exile lamps so Gawain and Percival must decide whether to guard the exiles or expose the stolen warrant at the gate.
Merlin bargains the silver for an heir
Merlin offers the silver compact for a named road and a sheltered heir, letting Morgan and the Lady of the Lake choose bounded peace or an open magical breach.

encounters.title: Camelot survives only as feudal enclaves answering to memory and armed claim rat

text_script.value:
At the frost-seal, Mordred breaks the oath-ring, takes Excalibur, and drives the point through the binding-road Arthur had tried to keep whole; Arthur does not pronounce the sword holy or lawful but only marks the moment when Camelot ceased to be a republic and became a chain of armed memories. Guinevere calls the unborn child unclaimed, Lancelot lowers his sword rather than judge the theft, Morgan turns the compact to black teal, Merlin accepts the pact he cannot save, and Gawain, Percival, Galahad, Kay, Bedivere, and the Lady of the Lake watch witnesses become wardens instead of witnesses. Arthur says, 'Then give me not the sword but the road it left open,' and the oath collapses into private vengeance, a forge of claimants, and enclaves that answer to names, debts, and graves rather than to a king.

Excalibur Betrayed: the sword is seized and misused, not by a savior but by a claimant who knows that authority is a ritual of possession, not a theorem of justice. Arthur's authority collapses into private vengeance; Camelot does not fall silently but fragments into enclaves that answer to names, grief, debts, and graves. The realm survives as memory, not law: each lord keeps a piece of the broken constitution, each exile carries a road, each shrine shelters a claim, and no single crown can again say who may give law to the rest.

encounters.title: At dawn, Mordred's claim has been laid openly on the table and Arthur must choos

text_script.value: Dawn found the Round Table stripped of its glitter, the stones of the tabletop showing pale seams where the oaths had been carved. Mordred laid a folded writ on the table's edge and said the court had already buried two crowns this week, one by choice and one by fear, and had not yet buried the third. Gawain answered that inheritance was an old habit that had never once protected the ordinary, while Lancelot, standing apart from both, said the law was a rope and the Round Table had been the only end of it anyone could still hold. Merlin did not declare his ancestors' suit at all; he only traced the crack in the table's edge and told Arthur that the shrine was not a question the dead could answer but a question the living were avoiding. Arthur looked at the writ, at Gawain's jaw, at the exiles' coats hanging in the doorway, and asked Mordred whether he wanted the crown or the peace.
Arthur yields the oath to Mordred
The crown passes lawfully into Mordred's hands, and Camelot enters a contested succession where the old institutions must be rebuilt under his claim.
Arthur swears the Round Table anew around both claims
The court attempts to bind Arthur and Mordred in a single covenant, but the renewal leaves the old oaths strained and Gawain and Lancelot divided over its cost.
The court offers Mordred the exile-witnessed road
Mordred is asked to leave Camelot with witness and charter, separating the crown from the shrine and sending the exiles into the road beyond the walls.

encounters.title: Mordred seeks limited lawful power over the Grail, exiles and succession rather

text_script.value: At the second bell the shrine doors were already sealed with wax, and Mordred laid his folded claim beside a sheaf of exiles' charters: if the old crown was a debt, he asked only to be allowed to pay its interest. Gawain answered that payment would still be payment, and the widows in the doorway were no interest anyone had consented to collect. Merlin did not judge him; he only weighed the pale seam in the tabletop and said the oath was not dead but starving, waiting for someone to decide what it was for. Arthur looked at the writ, the exiles' coats, and Mordred's unbowed head, and asked whether the claim wanted a king, a judge, or a witness.
Arthur ratifies Mordred as steward
Camelot gains a working ledger for widows, exiles and succession, but Arthur's peace is folded into Mordred's administration and the Round Table loses its unity.
Arthur separates the Grail shrine from the crown
The shrine becomes a civic trust under Merlin and Morgan, but the court can no longer answer who bears the Round Table's memory.
The court gives the exiles a road charter
Mordred's claim becomes road law, sending Gawain, Lancelot and the exiles into contested borders while Camelot empties toward memory.

encounters.title: Camelot has split into two councils with the shrine threshold contested: Arthur

text_script.value: On the third day the court ate in halves. Arthur's table kept its oath-lit lamps burning in the north chapel while Mordred's claimants feasted beneath the shrine stair, and Gawain carried the broken writ between the two rooms like a blade. Merlin did not open the shrine doors; he set a candle on the threshold and said the court had stopped being a kingdom the moment its law fed no one, while Lancelot answered that memory fed no one either. Morgan, who had not spoken since dawn, put her hand flat above the flame and called Mordred's claim 'the honest wound,' and Arthur asked him plainly whether the crown was a door he meant to walk through or a wall he meant to defend. Mordred answered that he would trade the crown for the doors, and Arthur said the doors were the only thing left that Camelot still owned.
Arthur grants Mordred a sanctuary charter
The claimants are given protected status under the shrine but not the crown, and the charter hardens Arthur's defense into a legally enforced schism that will need a successor to settle.
The Round Table is split into two tables
Camelot becomes two courts under one roof, and Gawain and Lancelot are forced to choose which table they sit at, emptying the shrine of its shared memory.
Merlin and Morgan audit the oaths aloud
The audit exposes which oaths were sworn in love, which in fear, and which were sworn to keep the exiles fed, leaving Camelot with a list of debts no one may lawfully close.

encounters.title: Camelot now confronts an empty ninth seat as Mordred's claim, Arthur's defense,

text_script.value: On the fourth day the ledgers were open and the names on them did not match the lamps. Arthur stood before the empty ninth seat while Mordred held the folded writ and said the oath could not be carried by the dead; Merlin said the shrine remembered, but it did not choose; Gawain named who could feed the exiles, Lancelot who could bear the blame, and Morgan asked whether the Round Table was a promise or a grave. Percival asked what would happen to the empty seat, and Mordred answered that it was the only place in Camelot where law still had room to grow.
Leave the ninth seat empty as a public question
Arthur gambles that the empty seat will hold the court together by forcing every claim to explain itself aloud, while Mordred can rule over the exiles but not over the table's memory.
Make the succession an open census
The court votes by public oath and debt rather than by blood, giving Mordred a legal claim and splitting the Round Table into a governing caucus and a remembering order.
Hold the shrine shut for one night
Merlin and Morgan seal the shrine with a night oath, forcing Arthur and Mordred to swear opposite sides while Bedivere and Percival carry the exile granaries beyond the walls.

encounters.title: Camelot is now divided across the shrine threshold: the empty ninth seat holds t

text_script.value: By the fifth day the granaries had gone quiet, and Arthur stood at the shrine threshold with the empty ninth seat visible behind him while Mordred stood one pace beyond the line and said that an oath no one ate from was only a funeral. Bedivere brought the exile ledgers â€” half of them, no names, only counts â€” and Percival said the counting was easier than the feeding. Lancelot asked who would remember the oath if the memory belonged to neither table, and Morgan answered that memory had never fed anyone, while Merlin asked the court to look at the empty seat and name, aloud, what it meant to keep. Arthur swore that the shrine would remain one shrine, and Mordred swore that no shrine could feed a people who no longer had bread.
Open the census at the threshold

The court reads the exiles' counts aloud at the shrine and must either feed them together or admit the oath has already failed them, splitting the Round Table into a feasting court and a remembering court.
Order a joint feast for the exiles
Arthur and Mordred must sit beneath one roof for one meal, forcing their oaths to touch hands publicly and leaving Lancelot and Gawain to carry the division back to the Round Table afterward.
Open the shrine for one hour
Merlin and Morgan seal the shrine for one hour and both sides enter, forcing Mordred's claim and Arthur's defense to be sworn inside the shrine itself and recorded by the exile ledgers.

encounters.title: On the sixth day, the seal-light is thin, the exiles' counts are fixed and unfor

text_script.value: By the sixth day the shrine's seal-light had burned thin and the ledgers no longer needed to be counted twice. Arthur stood at the head of the table with his oath-ring bare in his fist, while Mordred walked the outside of the ninth seat and read aloud the writ he had cut from the old charter, saying that a crown left empty was a debt nobody paid. Gawain struck his bargain with the exiles at dawn, grain for grain against silence, and Lancelot, who had buried his own loyalty in that grain, answered that debt paid with bread was still debt. Merlin said the shrine remembered every oath ever sworn to it, and Morgan answered that memory was only a lamp that never emptied, and Bedivere set the exile counts down where both men could see them: fewer bellies fed than there were lamps lit. Percival asked whether the Round Table could be a table if no one was certain who was at the head of it, and Mordred looked at the empty seat and said that a table without its empty seat was only a dining hall.
Let Mordred sit, bound by the shrine oath

Mordred takes the ninth seat but is forced to swear the shrine oath in public and feed the exiles first, splitting the Round Table into a legal throne and a feasting order that may still hold together or fracture cleanly.
Write a joint charter of sharing

Arthur and Mordred bind themselves to a shared charter with Gawain guarding the grain and Lancelot guarding the memory, but the court must now rule as two kings under one shrine or dissolve the table entirely.
Open the gates to the exiles
Bedivere and Percival carry the grain beyond the walls and the court chooses whether to follow the exiles outward or hold the shrine and lose the people it was built to serve.

encounters.title: On the seventh day the exiles have left Camelot, the ninth seat is unfilled and

text_script.value: On the seventh day the exiles walked out of the gates in their last thin numbers, leaving their counts behind on the shrine step like stones after a river. Arthur stood before the empty ninth seat and heard Lancelot say that bread and memory could not both be carried by one hand, and Morgan answered that neither could be carried by two. Merlin asked what the table meant now that no one was certain who would sit at its head, and Mordred, still beyond the threshold line, said that a crown was only a promise and a promise needed someone willing to keep it. The court had one day, one oath, and nowhere left to stand.
Yield the ninth seat to Mordred
Arthur formally hands the crown and the ninth seat to Mordred, making Camelot a Mordred-ruled kingdom whose shrine oath and Round Table must now survive under a claim Arthur once refused.
Feed the exiles from the shrine stores
The court spends the shrine's own reserves to feed the leaving exiles, splitting the Round Table between those who will eat the oath and those who will keep it.
Seal the Round Table
Merlin and Morgan bind the Round Table for one day, freezing the court's choices until the succession is settled and the shrine light goes out to mark the truce.

encounters.title: A sealed Round Table has turned law, bread, and memory into competing claims, wi

text_script.value: The seal did not make the court quiet; it made the choices small enough to see. Merlin lifted one corner of the shrine cloth and found the oath written backward, so that every word named a debt rather than a king, while Mordred stood inside the threshold and said he did not want the crown so much as the writ that kept it honest. Gawain read the grain count aloud, Lancelot answered that the shrine could not keep two kinds of promise at once, and Morgan warned that a sealed table was a tomb with good manners. Arthur looked at the empty ninth seat and had to decide whether it was a place of law, a grave, or a table that still fed people.
Let Mordred inherit the writ and the gates
Mordred becomes lawful keeper of the writ and the exile gates, and Arthur's peace is replaced by an obligation to keep ordinary people fed.
Make Arthur a witness, not a ruler
Arthur signs a two-handed charter in which Mordred rules the table while Arthur guards the memory of its promises.
Break the seal into a ledger of debts
Merlin and Morgan turn the shrine into a public ledger, so legitimacy comes from what the court pays rather than from what it wears.

encounters.title: The shrine ledger is public and the shrine light is dying; Mordred holds the wri

text_script.value: The seal came off at dawn and the ledger stayed. Mordred had the debts read aloud before the ninth seat, and for the first time in living memory a count did not settle who would eat but only who had already eaten; Gawain stood at the threshold and found the exiles' names already written in his own hand, which he had not meant to write. Lancelot said the crown was a promise and the people were the only thing left that had ever kept one, while Morgan closed her fingers around the shrine light, now dim as a coal, and said that a ruined table was not the failure of the table but its last honest shape. Merlin, half-blind, asked whether the oath would still hold if no one any longer remembered what it was for.
Break the ninth seat open
Arthur breaks the sealed seat into an open door, ending the Round Table's claim to legitimacy and beginning a different kingdom born from ruin under Mordred's writ.
Let the exiles re-seat themselves
The exiles and their keepers set a new table beyond the gates, leaving the Round Table behind as a shrine and a memory rather than a ruling thing.
Keep the seal as a sacrament
Merlin and Morgan bind the table again as a holy memory, so Mordred rules beneath a sacred vacancy and the Round Table survives as an oath rather than a power.

encounters.title: Mordred holds the writ and gates, the exiles wait outside with bread and names,

text_script.value: The exiles came with bread still wrapped in linen and stood beyond the gates as if the Round Table were a wall they no longer owed. Mordred set the writ on an empty altar stone and asked who would guard the debt now that the crown had stopped paying it. Arthur said he would witness, and no more, while Lancelot answered that a witness who would not feed the hungry was only a clerk with a crown. Gawain read the dead names aloud, Bedivere marked the broken seat with ash instead of a sword, and Merlin told Morgan that the last light was not fading so much as becoming smaller and harder to lie with.
Seal the exile writ
Mordred authorizes the gates to a standing exile household, replacing Arthur's peace with a law that must feed people at the edge of Camelot.
Make the ledger a court
Arthur refuses the throne but authorizes the shrine-ledger as a public court, leaving Mordred to govern by debt while Arthur keeps the promise visible.
Close the shrine
Merlin and Morgan seal the shrine as a holy ruin, so Camelot survives as a memory while the exiles decide whether to follow it or carry it away.

encounters.title: Mordred holds the writ and gates with the exiles inside the walls, Arthur is a w

text_script.value: The exiles filed through the gates at noon with their names already written on the writ, and Mordred set bread before each household and asked them to speak their names into the shrine ledger. Arthur read the ninth page and found his own signature written in a borrowed hand, a lie that held the peace better than the crown ever had. Lancelot said the ledger would outlive the table, while Merlin answered that a ledger which feeds no one is only a list of names, and Morgan closed her fingers around the shrine light as if it were a coal she could still carry into the crowd.
Feed the ledger
Mordred feeds the exiles publicly under the writ, so Camelot becomes a provisioned state in which the Round Table survives only as a law of bread and names.
Take the ninth seat
Arthur returns to the sealed seat and reopens the legitimacy crisis, forcing Mordred, Gawain, and Lancelot to choose between law, loyalty, and the promise to the people.
Open the dying shrine
Merlin and Morgan spend the shrine light among the exiles, ending the sacred vacancy and binding the old magic to the feedings of ordinary people.

encounters.title: The ninth page bears a borrowed Arthurian signature, Mordred claims authority th

text_script.value: At the shrine ledger, the ninth page kept catching the light as if it were still a wound. Mordred read the borrowed signature aloud, not as an accusation but as proof that a law could survive its author, while Arthur set his glove beside the page and refused to call it a seal. Gawain said the table was no longer a seat but a debt, Lancelot answered that a debt kept warm was not a crown, and Bedivere read the names the table had already lost. Merlin lifted the dying coal toward the exiles; Morgan closed her hand around it and asked who would carry the light if the room went dark.
Make the witness a covenant
Arthur lets his refusal be spoken as covenant rather than seal, so Mordred governs through a promise that must be renewed before every feeding.
Break the ninth page
Gawain and Percival expose the borrowed hand, ending the fraudulent legitimacy but leaving the exiles to choose lawlessness, flight, or a new charter.
Carry the coal out
Merlin and Morgan carry the shrine light past the gates, turning Camelot's law into a practice of feeding, names, and small endurance outside the shrine.

encounters.title: The covenant is spoken but unsealed, the shrine coal has been carried toward the

text_script.value: Before the opened gate, Mordred set the ledger on a stone bench and spoke the covenant aloud: bread, names, and witnesses, not a seal. Arthur stood beside the ninth page and answered, 'Then do not seal us; feed us or leave us.' Merlin lowered the brazier toward the exiles while Morgan kept one hand around the coal and asked, 'If the table is gone, who carries its discipline?' Lancelot said the kingdom had become too small for pride, Gawain kept one eye on the oaths, and Percival began naming the dead who had already been buried inside the writ.
Renew the feedings
Mordred turns the gate into a permanent provisioning office, making the Round Table survive as a public obligation of food, witness, and memory.
Carry the coal out
Merlin and Morgan move the shrine light beyond the shrine itself, binding old magic to household survival rather than to the seat of the realm.
Test the borrowed hand
Gawain and Percival open the fraud publicly, forcing Mordred to choose between exposure, a clean charter, or a new claim outside the old table.

encounters.title: The exiles have arrived at the threshold of the hall, Mordred offers a lawful su

text_script.value: Before first light the exiles came through the gate carrying their bundles and their silences, and Mordred asked Arthur to sit at the foot of the empty table and hear what the chairs would mean when no king owned them. Arthur stood and said he would not be the author of the last lie the Round Table ever told. Gawain named what was missing from the empty seats — not rank, but a reason to gather — while Lancelot said that reason could be a kitchen table, a shared bread, a name spoken over the dead, and he would not wait for the word king. Morgan asked what the table had been built to survive, and Merlin answered that it had been built to outlast the man who made it, and Percival began reading the names of those who would not return.
Seat the exiles
Mordred declares the empty chairs wards seated by need rather than lineage, so the table survives as a common good and Arthur must either yield his crown's meaning or break it.
Speak the covenant as law
Arthur and Mordred speak the unsealed covenant into a public law, and the exiles become its standing witnesses rather than its recipients.
Close the Round Table
Arthur rules the table dead, leaving Camelot to live as a just community without its emblem, with the exiles choosing to follow the oath or the table's absence.

encounters.title: The unsealed law has become an active test: Mordred can make the order visible a

text_script.value: Percival read the names aloud in a voice meant for the living, and Arthur answered that a name spoken over hunger was not a memorial but an appointment. Mordred set both palms on the open charter and said, 'If the king leaves, let the writ not leave his children,' while Gawain demanded the price of calling that law. Morgan kept the last coal near her wrist and asked what such a law would do when no one was left to fear it.
Open the ledger
Mordred makes the office public, so oaths, debts, and exile rights are read aloud daily and the Round Table survives as an auditable institution.
Sever the crown
Arthur stops ruling by title and instead swears to the exiles that no future king may keep the table without their signatures.
Carry the light
Merlin and Morgan carry the shrine flame outward, tying the law to households and roads instead of to Camelot's seat.

encounters.title: The covenant has become a portable test: it can survive as law for exiles and ro

text_script.value: At the second reading of the covenant, the exiles no longer stood as a queue outside the threshold but as a ring of named debts inside the hall, and Merlin held the shrine flame low until Arthur answered that he did not trust a law that could not be carried by people who had never loved Camelot. Mordred laid the charter flat and said that if the crown was a claim on the table, then the table could be a claim on everyone who swore to feed it, and Gawain countered that a law so useful would still need someone who could be made to answer for its failure. Morgan asked whether Lancelot, whose oath was divided, could be trusted to swear, and Lancelot answered that he could swear as plainly as he could feed, which was the only kind of oath he had left. Percival read the names aloud again, and Bedivere answered that the names were not a verdict but a list of places the law would have to live next.
Carry the law onward
Mordred, Percival, and Bedivere carry the covenant beyond Camelot, making the exiles the law's witnesses and turning the Round Table into a travelling shrine of need.
Seal the signatures
Arthur makes the exiles co-authors of the covenant, forcing every future king to keep their names in the charter or lose the Round Table's legitimacy.
Let Mordred rule
Arthur cedes the crown to Mordred's lawful claim, but the oath, relic-shrine, and court become a hard choice between stability for the table and survival for those outside it.

encounters.title: The Round Table is being rebuilt as an auditable covenant, but succession, relic

text_script.value: By the second bell the charter no longer lay on the high table but moved from hand to hand, read aloud over the exiles' names as the lamps guttered. Mordred asked if the crown could survive the Round Table, and Arthur answered that the crown was only a claim; the table was the claim's sworn house. Merlin lifted the shrine flame just enough to show the Grail's reflection trembling on the charter, while Morgan said that what cannot be refused will soon be worshipped. Gawain answered for Lancelot that a divided oath is still an oath if it feeds people, and Bedivere answered for the shrine that the flame itself had become a door.
Ward the shrine
The Grail flame is split among keeper-homes, so succession can change hands but the shrine no longer belongs to one crown.
Grant Mordred kingship
Arthur formally yields the crown to Mordred's lawful claim, opening a hard choice between Camelot's unity and the exiles' survival.
Publish the debts
The exiles keep public seats and signatures, but the charter becomes a daily test of which king is willing to lose more power than he gains.

encounters.title: The court is deciding whether succession is a hereditary claim, a shared debt, o

text_script.value: On the last day of the old calendar, Mordred unrolled the charter beside the shrine and asked Arthur to say what a king was for when his heir was named in the same breath as his enemy. Merlin held the Grail flame against Arthur's face and said succession was not a bloodline but a burden repeated until it became habit. Morgan laughed low at the idea that the crown could be refused without the table, then knelt and admitted that refusal had only seemed honorable while it stayed untested. Gawain read the exiles' debts aloud as a ledger rather than a eulogy, Lancelot set his own divided oath beside the shrine without naming it, and Bedivere said that if the Round Table still mattered it would have to answer for what it left outside the door.
Crown Mordred by debt
Arthur lawfully yields the crown to Mordred only while the exiles remain named in the charter, so the table becomes contested memory rather than an untouchable throne.
Keep the table, refuse the crown
Arthur refuses transfer and seals the Round Table as an ideal, leaving Mordred's claim, the exiles, and the shrine to survive outside the courthouse.
Make the shrine the heir
The Grail flame passes among keeper-homes while the crown becomes one claim among many, turning succession into custody rather than dominion.

encounters.title: The court now faces a choice between splitting shrine and succession, ceding kin

text_script.value: By candle-lowering the exiles filed into the court and set their names on the Round Table in order, from the least to the last, until the table seemed less a circle than a balance. Arthur asked Mordred whether he would rule for the crown or against it, and Mordred answered that he would rule for the debt, whether the table stayed whole or broke. Morgan laughed low at loyalty that had no arithmetic, while Merlin touched the Grail flame and said it would not take sides so much as remember whoever touched it. Gawain read the exiles' ledger aloud as law rather than grief, Lancelot set his divided oath on the table without naming it, and Bedivere said the shrine would outlast both king and table.
Split the shrine
The Grail flame passes among keeper-homes and Arthur and Mordred become oath-partners rather than successors, so kingship becomes custody while the exiles' names keep public seats.
Let Mordred rule with public seats
Mordred takes the crown, but the Round Table survives as a common court where exiles, widows and crown all retain seats and signatures, making the transfer a test of lawful rule.
Break the Round Table
Arthur lets the table break and be remade outside court, ending kingship as one house's monopoly while the shrine, debts and exiles continue in a different form.

encounters.title: The court is deciding whether Mordred's rule can be made lawful by public audit,

text_script.value: The morning after the ledger arrived as thin gold rain over the broken seats, and the court stopped speaking in prophecy until Mordred asked each of them to name what he could carry away. Arthur said a king could carry law, Gawain said a knight could carry debts, Lancelot admitted he could carry only the cost of choosing, and Percival whispered that an exile could carry no one but himself. Merlin held the flame so low that it seemed to be listening; Morgan leaned on the shattered rim and said an ideal was easy until someone had to feed the widows it named. Bedivere set the empty throne outside the shrine, and Mordred watched the flame bend toward the exiles rather than the crown.
Bind Mordred to public audit
Mordred accepts the crown only as a revocable office under exiles, widows, shrine-keepers and the table's ledger, so law may survive even if dominion does not.
Hand the flame to keeper-homes
The Grail becomes shared custody among outer shrines and keeper-homes, freeing Arthur from sole possession while Mordred must govern without claiming the relic's meaning.
Make the table testimony
The Round Table is broken into named stones and public witnesses, leaving Camelot to rule as a ruined archive that must answer for the exiles it excluded.

encounters.title: Camelot must decide whether Mordred can hold the crown as a public, revocable cu

text_script.value: By the shrine gate, Mordred laid the ledger flat and let the flame lean across its pages as though it had already read the exiles' names. Arthur asked what law could become if a seat was empty but the debt was not, and Gawain answered that law was an argument for staying in a ruin. Lancelot set his divided oath on the ledger like a counterweight, Morgan called a throne a convenience for people who had not yet chosen, and Merlin said the flame remembered the ones who carried its weight. Then Percival stepped forward and told Mordred that the exile who came would not be asked whether he had earned a seat; he would be asked what he could refuse.
Make Mordred a revocable custodian
Mordred keeps the crown only as an audited custody, sworn to be unseated if he cannot keep seats, flame and exile debts public.
Move the shrine to exile-wards
The flame and shrine leave the court and divide among outer keeper-homes, so law becomes mobile but the crown loses its central sacred witness.
Seal the table as witness-stones
The broken Round Table becomes a public archive of oaths outside court, making Camelot a shrine of testimony rather than a throne.

encounters.title: Camelot is deciding whether Mordred's claim can become a lawful, revocable custo

text_script.value: The court gathers beneath the gate-arch while the ledger lies open like a tongue of gold under the first rain. Mordred says the crown is not a title but a duty to be checked, Arthur answers that duty has no shelter if it cannot say what it will lose, and Gawain names the widows and exiles who would be erased if legitimacy stopped at the threshold. Lancelot admits his loyalty can no longer be the old oath whole, Merlin warns that a flame divided too soon may stop meaning anything, Morgan says magic should answer the excluded rather than impress the included, and Bedivere lifts the throne toward the outer ward while Percival asks each of them what they would leave behind if the court had to choose one truth.
Bind Mordred to public audit
Mordred receives the crown only as a revocable office audited by exiles, widows, shrine-keepers and witnesses, so dominion survives as accountable custody rather than royal will.
Split the flame to keeper-homes
The shrine and flame leave Camelot and are divided among outer keeper-homes, weakening the central court but making the sacred object answer ordinary households.
Open the table as testimony archive
The broken Round Table becomes a public archive of oaths, exile-names and broken promises, forcing Camelot to govern as a ruined witness rather than a throne.

encounters.title: Camelot survives only as a relic-court under Mordred's forced legitimacy, with t

text_script.value:
At the shrine-gate the audited custody failed before it could breathe: the flame guttered, the exile-wards gave no answer, and Gawain laughed once, bitterly, at the word 'public'. Mordred stood in the empty seat and did not ask to be blessed; he said kinship and force were older than a table that had promised to stay level. Arthur did not forbid him, only watched the Round Table lose its edges, seat by seat, into a shrine of memory. Lancelot set his divided oath down like a coin, Merlin let the old magic fall silent, Morgan called the ruin a kingdom to be kept by those who remembered it, and Percival understood that the exiles would now be named on stones beyond the gate, not admitted within it.

Mordred does not become innocent; he becomes unquestionable. The crown passes not as a blessed office but as a family claim stiffened by force, announced in a ruin that still calls itself a court. The Round Table is kept because it is beautiful and broken, a relic-shrine where knights gather to remember what law once promised and to admire the shape of a freedom they no longer govern. Camelot endures, but only as a mourning monument: law remains visible as a stone, the Grail as a flicker, the exiles as names beyond the wall, and the old republic survives as a cult of memory rather than a living order.

encounters.title: At the east gate at dawn, the Grail road begins as a contest over whether the cu

text_script.value: At first light the empty cup sat on a flat stone at the road's mouth while the east sky burned violet and gold. Percival lifted his voice so the exiles outside could hear: 'The Grail is not a prize, it is a debt we can still pay.' Galahad answered that debts had been ruined by claimants, and asked whether purity could enter a court that was already broken. Merlin leaned close to the cup, touched it with two fingers, and said the light in it was not hope but an instruction, and that following it would cost the crown its oldest answers. Arthur hesitated, then asked each who would carry the road outward.
Galahad carries the cup outward
Galahad takes the Grail onto the east road, and the court splits into those who follow him and those who swear to protect the crown behind him.
Percival carries the cup and names the exiles
The road becomes an exile-witnessed covenant, turning the Grail quest into a test of whether sacred knowledge serves the ordinary people outside the walls.
Arthur seals the shrine and holds the crown
Arthur refuses the road, the shrine holds its silence, and the realm remains a court bound to memory rather than a kingdom remade by the Grail.

encounters.title: At a threshold shrine the Grail road is becoming a civic rite, with Arthur torn

text_script.value: By midmorning the road had narrowed into a shrine-court of broken thresholds, and the exiles lined the path with their dead tokens rather than banners. Percival set the Grail on a threshold stone and asked the crowd to speak one loss they would not surrender, while Galahad kept his hand on the cup and refused to call it a victory. 'I did not come to bless a throne,' Galahad said; 'I came to prove what a debt owes.' Morgan le Fay glided between the lines and smiled at the ring of light, saying the old magic could still make an order, or only make one purer idol. Merlin told Arthur that the test was no longer whether the cup healed Camelot, but whether Camelot would let a wound in the ordinary world become law.
Percival names the exiles into the covenant
The Grail is witnessed by the exiles, and legitimacy moves from court inheritance to a spoken debt owed to ordinary people.
Galahad asks Arthur to pledge the shrine to widows and exiles
Purity becomes a binding order rather than a royal gift, forcing Arthur to accept a shrine governed by oaths outside his own house.
Morgan offers the old magic to seal the road
The road gains a disciplined ward, but the Grail risks being trapped inside a spell instead of moving into ordinary life.

encounters.title: At a forded shrine-road, the Grail stands inside a public covenant: Galahad urge

text_script.value: At the ford of black stones, the cup had been set into the threshold rather than upon it, so that every step toward the road now passed through the debt. Galahad knelt with mud on his gauntlets and asked Arthur to bind the shrine to widows, exiles and witnesses before he asked to rule it; Arthur heard his title fail and was offered a harder one. Percival leaned over the water and named the villages that had already buried their hope, while Morgan smiled at the old light and said the ward could hold the road open or lock it shut as neatly as a church door.
Galahad binds the shrine to the exiles
Arthur must swear the Grail-shrine to widows, exiles and witnesses, moving legitimacy from royal inheritance into a public order that outlives the court.
Percival sends the cup toward the villages
The quest becomes a chain of ordinary-life tests, carrying hope and suspicion into places where the court can no longer control the meaning of the Grail.
Morgan seals the road with the old ward
Merlin and Morgan hold a disciplined guardian over the path, but the Grail becomes protected by force and may be read by ordinary people as a relic of domination rather than justice.

encounters.title: At the forked shrine-road, the Grail is between two fates: a binding public orde

text_script.value: The forked shrine road had become a narrow trial of lamps, and the cup lay on a black threshold where the ward-light and the village path touched. Arthur heard his crown-title echo as Galahad named the debt aloud, while Percival read the exiles' names from tokens worn on their sleeves; Morgan lowered a veil of pale gold over the path, saying the ward could keep the road clean or turn it into a prison of beautiful light. Merlin answered that the old magic would hold whatever order was given to it, and that the question was now whether Camelot would become a place where ruins were law, or only a shrine that survived them.
Percival and Galahad seat the exiles in the witness ring
Arthur must accept the cup as a debt witnessed by those outside the court, forcing succession to be argued in front of ordinary people rather than behind royal walls.
Percival leads the cup down the village path
The Grail leaves the shrine for the first villages, carrying hope and suspicion into ordinary life where the court can neither rule it nor keep it safe.
Morgan keeps the ward at half-light
The road is protected but not free: Morgan and Merlin preserve a discipline that ordinary people may experience as justice, or as a beautiful cage around sacred power.

encounters.title: The Grail is suspended over a forked road, forcing Camelot to choose between a w

text_script.value: The road splits before the shrine into a silver strand and a gold one, and the cup hangs between them like a verdict not yet given. Percival held two tokens to his lips and said the villages had already buried hope once this year, while Galahad answered that the cup would only heal what it was allowed to witness. Morgan smiled at the gold strand and said it could keep the road safe as a locked chapel, or let the light wander like a forbidden word, and Arthur heard his own crown answer neither question cleanly. Bedivere kept the only witness-mark he had made: a blackened thumbprint on the threshold where a widow's brother had once been taken.
Seat exiles as covenant-keepers
Arthur is forced to swear succession in front of those who are not of the court, so the throne becomes a public bond instead of an inherited title.
Send Percival down the village path
The cup leaves the shrine before it is fully known, carrying hope and suspicion into named farms and ruined holdings where promises must be tested daily.
Open one eye in the old ward
Merlin and Morgan let one narrow channel of light pass while keeping the road bounded, creating a protected path that can be seen as justice, or as a beautiful cage.

encounters.title: The Grail rests in the lower shrine hall between public covenant, village life,

text_script.value: In the lower shrine hall, Galahad lowered the cup until it answered the light rather than the court, and Percival read the village-tokens aloud: a widow's seed, a ferryman's debt, a name whose grave stood above the water. Arthur heard his title soften into a questionâ€”what if the throne survived as a custom of care, not a title of inheritance? Lady of the Lake said the Grail kept the memory of every time it was asked to choose, while Morgan and Merlin let one emerald cord of light tremble between the stair and the gate.
Name the cup as a covenant
Arthur must publicly renew the succession before widows, exiles, and village-kin, turning the throne into a witnessed bond rather than an inherited mark.
Send the cup to the first water-villages
Percival carries the Grail into named wards where promises must be paid daily, and the court can neither rule it nor keep it safe.
Keep one bounded channel open
Morgan and Merlin hold a narrow road of light open, preserving order as discipline or as a beautiful cage.

encounters.title: The Grail stands at the shrine threshold with a village ledger and a pledge unsp

text_script.value: At the shrine gate, Bedivere brought a ledger of the villages who had sent tokens, and Percival read out the names until the court could no longer pretend the Grail belonged only to Camelot. Arthur found his crown heavy enough to lean on, and when he asked what the throne would be once the cup was witnessed, Galahad answered that it would be a debt owed aloud. Morgan le Fay leaned close and said the old ward could keep the road safe, but she could not swear it would keep the peace, and Merlin countered that a kingdom is not made safe by walls but by the promise to repair them. Arthur said he would rather be judged by those who owed him nothing than praised by those who owed him everything, and the cup in the dark behind them answered with a single low pulse.
Swear the succession before the villagers
Arthur gives the cup to the witnesses rather than the crown, so the succession becomes a public bond that must be renewed against failure, not inheritance.
Open the ward one narrow eye
Merlin and Morgan hold a bounded channel open so that one protected road serves the villages while the rest of the frontier is locked away.
Let Percival carry the cup into the farms
Percival leaves the shrine with the Grail and the ledger, and the court must trust that a path can be walked without being owned.

encounters.title: At the shrine threshold, Camelot must turn the Grail from inherited power into a

text_script.value: On the threshold between court and valley, Bedivere laid the ledger flat while Arthur looked at a succession that had no throne-room form left. Arthur asked what kind of kingdom would wake if the cup refused to crown anyone, and Galahad answered that it would wake as a promise heard by people who did not already love the palace. Percival said a widow should be allowed to say no, and Morgan said every no would have to be heard somewhere. Merlin replied that the promise could be kept by law, by light, or by both, but never by invisibility.
Renew the covenant before the villages
Arthur makes the succession a public bond that can be remade after failure, placing the crown in front of villagers rather than above them.
Hold one guarded ward-road
Merlin and Morgan keep one protected channel open for supplies and refuge, but access becomes a controlled privilege rather than a free path.
Let Percival carry the cup down the valley
Percival and Bedivere walk the Grail and ledger toward the wards, moving Camelot's center out of the shrine and into the promised places.

encounters.title: At the shrine threshold, Camelot must turn the Grail into a walkable covenant, a

text_script.value: By the third dawn after the ledger was read, the road had split into three claims: a covenant chalked on a slate, a ward-gate chained but humming, and a path worn by feet that had not come to Camelot. Galahad set the Grail on the shrine floor and asked whether the cup would remember the village names if the court tried to make them heirs. Morgan named the cost of a guarded road in burnt orchards, Merlin named the cost of an open path in unanswered oaths, and Arthur answered with a question about whose failure the kingdom would be built to heal. Bedivere copied the names while Percival watched the cup's light bend toward the field beyond the gate.
Make the covenant a walkable oath
The court writes succession into village duties and marks the crown by what is kept after failure, not by what is inherited.
Bind the ward to one proven road
Merlin and Morgan keep a narrow protected channel open so supplies move while the rest of the frontier stays walled.
Carry the cup into the farms
Percival and Bedivere take the Grail and ledger down the road, forcing Camelot to answer for a kingdom whose center is no longer only the shrine.

encounters.title: The Grail is now carried past the shrine threshold into the open valley, with a

text_script.value: By midmorning the cup had left the shrine stair and stood on the valley floor, and Percival, not Arthur, was the one holding it, which unsettled every witness. A widow in the field line called out that her husband's share of the oath was not on any ledger, and Galahad answered that the cup would hold it only if someone wrote it down. Merlin touched the Grail's rim and reported that it did not glow toward the court; it leaned toward whatever place most needed to be heard, and right now that was the field. Morgan asked what would happen when the leaning changed, and Percival answered that the kingdom would have to follow it, which was the part nobody at Camelot had budgeted for. Arthur opened the ledger to a fresh page and wrote nothing yet, because the page had to stay empty until the village spoke its own name.
Open the page for the widow's claim
Arthur writes her uncounted debt into the covenant as a standing public obligation, so succession becomes a duty to be re-kept after failure rather than a title passed down.
Run one hearing with law and light together
Galahad and Merlin split one public audit into two columns, law and Grail, so Camelot learns what the oath covers and what it leaves beyond reach.
Let Morgan ring the cup's bell down the valley
Morgan sounds the Grail bell so the villages hear Camelot's claim, but the bell also carries whatever the villages answer back, making Camelot accountable to a voice it did not choose.

encounters.title: Camelot stands at the ford with the Grail leaning toward village needs, facing a

text_script.value: The valley bells answered in pieces: a latch lifted, a goat bell, a name called twice and swallowed. Galahad held the cup low while Arthur read the ledger aloud, and Percival watched the light bend not toward the shrine but toward the ford where people were already arguing over bread. Morgan said, 'A safe road is still a wall,' and Merlin answered, 'An open road is still a debt,' and Percival asked, 'What if the oath is both at once?' Arthur closed the ledger, then opened it again, because the court could not decide whether the Grail should teach law or be carried as a common burden.
Write law and want in one public census
Arthur forces the court and villages to name what is owed and what is needed in the same record, so the Grail becomes an ongoing obligation rather than a shrine relic.
Make the ford a self-judging ward
Morgan, Merlin, and Percival set terms at the crossing, letting local voices judge safety and need while Arthur keeps the crown from becoming the only voice in the kingdom.
Carry the Grail down the farm road
Percival and Bedivere leave Camelot for the wards with the cup and ledger, forcing the court to govern from distance rather than from a seat at the center.

encounters.title: The Grail has moved from shrine to farm road, and Camelot must decide whether sa

text_script.value: On the farm road the Grail stopped glowing and began to lean, as if listening. Percival held it low while Bedivere marked a small notch beside each village that had spoken; Arthur stood where the road bent, and for the first time he did not read the covenant back, he asked the villagers what it should be called. Morgan le Fay said that a ledger without weather was already a kind of oath; Merlin answered that a cup without names was only a treasure, and Percival told them both that the kingdom would not be healed by purity alone, but by whoever could carry the cup without making it a god.
Keep a road ledger of spoken needs
Percival and Bedivere write every ward's need beside the cup's path, turning succession into an ongoing round of testimony rather than a crown passed down.
Set law and Grail as one rule
Arthur funds public hearings under a two-voice rule so safety law and sacred need must both answer before Camelot can move again.
Let Morgan test the road's old lock
Morgan and Merlin bargain with the road itself, forcing the court to choose between an open gift, a bounded passage, or a forbidden crossing.

encounters.title: The road ledger is weighing law, oath, and village need together, and the Grail'

text_script.value: On the second dusk the ledger was heavier than the cup, and Percival read the wards aloud until the court learned to argue in voices outside itself. Galahad said the Grail should be carried as pure witness and not as a symbol, while Morgan answered that a witness sworn only to itself was a landlord in holy dress. Arthur watched the ford where three families had drawn the line between bread and oath, and Merlin leaned over the cup's rim and murmured that the old lock was not broken at the road but in the promise that held the road, and that to ask the Grail for healing was to ask it to choose a politics.
Open a ward court of witnesses
Arthur lets villagers, not the Round Table, read the covenant aloud, so succession becomes a recurring hearing instead of a crown ceremony.
Ask Galahad to witness the Grail's answer
Galahad and Percival descend toward the shrine to receive the cup's sign of what it can heal, making the ending a question of evidence rather than relic triumph.
Test the old promise with Morgan
Morgan and Merlin expose the locked promise inside the road, forcing the court to decide whether the Grail may be asked to open a bargain or only to witness one.

encounters.title: The wards now speak in relays and the court must decide whether the covenant is

text_script.value: On the third dusk the ledger had stopped being a list of wards and become a choir, each village voice answering the last until the court could no longer pretend to hear itself. Galahad knelt beside the cup and said it had stopped asking what it was for and begun asking who it was for, while Morgan le Fay answered that an oath sworn to a crowd is a different thing from an oath sworn to a face. Bedivere read the final entry aloud — blank — and Merlin told them both that the Grail had never answered a question, only a need, and that the difference was the whole question.
Make the wards seal the covenant
Arthur swears the covenant as a recurring public hearing, so succession becomes an annual act of testimony before the Round Table rather than a crown passed down.
Send Galahad and Percival to the shrine
The two knights descend to ask the cup directly what it can heal, turning the ending into evidence gathered rather than a relic restored.
Let Morgan test the road's promise
Morgan and Merlin expose the locked bargain inside the road, forcing Camelot to decide whether the Grail may open a passage or only witness one.

encounters.title: The wards now carry live testimony into Camelot, the cup refuses simple triumph,

text_script.value: On the third dawn after the blank line, the court was no longer a circle but a scale with no fixed pivot. Galahad lifted the cup and felt it dim instead of blaze, while Percival read the recovered entry aloud: the road remembers its own names. Morgan asked why a healing relic should be asked to hold a kingdom together, and Merlin answered that the Grail had never been a temple for holiness but a weighing floor where need, debt, and oath all left footprints. Arthur watched two exiles return under oath and saw the Round Table becoming a hearing room before it was a throne.
Open the annual ward hearing
Arthur turns succession into an annual testimony before the wards, so the kingdom is judged by need and oath rather than by crown ceremony.
Send Galahad and Percival to the shrine
The two knights carry the cup and ward rolls down to the shrine to seek a sign of what can be healed, turning the ending into evidence rather than relic triumph.
Test the road's old bargain
Morgan and Merlin expose the locked promise inside the road, forcing Camelot to decide whether the Grail may open a passage or only witness one.

encounters.title: Camelot stands between a recurring ward-hearing, a descent to the shrine for evi

text_script.value: At first light the wards had stopped behaving like bells and begun behaving like witnesses, each one repeating a debt rather than a warning. Percival held the cup close enough to feel its weight change from treasure to arithmetic, while Galahad found that the inscription on the inner rim now read backward whenever the court spoke of victory. Morgan rose slowly and said, "You are not looking for a relic, you are looking for an excuse not to govern," and Merlin answered, "Then let governors feel what it is like to be judged." Bedivere opened the ledger and read the last line aloud; it was blank, but beneath the blank there was a smaller mark shaped like a key, a road, and a hollow footprint all at once.
Arthur makes the ward-hearing binding
Succession is declared a recurring testimony before the Round Table, and Camelot becomes an order of public judgment rather than a court of inherited rank.
Galahad and Percival carry the cup to the shrine
The two knights move beyond argument to ask the shrine what can be healed, and the ending turns from restoration into evidence with a price.
Morgan and Merlin test the road's locked promise
The old bargain is exposed before all of Camelot, forcing the court to choose whether the Grail opens a passage or only witnesses one.

encounters.title: Camelot faces a succession rite that can become a public hearing, a descent to t

text_script.value: At the hour when the wards woke, the Round Table had become a floor of witness-stones: each name spoken made the Grail settle deeper instead of blaze. Galahad set the cup on the seal-stone and found it heavier whenever Arthur used the word peace; Percival, beside him, read the fresh inscription until it answered in a second tongue. Morgan stood at the threshold with a black latch and asked why the court kept asking the cup to certify the throne instead of the names behind it, and Merlin answered that a relic that needs no reckoning is already a weapon of rank. Bedivere opened the exile roll and read only the three debts that still stood unpaid, while the two exiles beyond the gate answered from the dark before any oath was spoken.
Arthur makes the hearing binding
Succession is judged as recurring testimony, and unpaid debts move from the gate to the throne.
Galahad and Percival carry the cup down
The knights carry the Grail and the ward-rolls below the shrine to find what can be healed without declaring victory.
Morgan and Merlin expose the latch
The court witnesses the road's old promise and must choose whether the Grail opens a passage or only names its cost.

encounters.title: Camelot now holds shrine evidence naming unpaid lives and an unmarked road, and

text_script.value: In the descent beneath the shrine, the Grail returned an image that was neither crown nor victory, but an unmade promise with someone missing from it. Galahad lifted the cup until Percival flinched and kept his hand on the seal-stone, and the inscription changed from victory to names, from names to one hollow road. Morgan said the relic was not choosing Camelot but asking which people were allowed to answer, while Merlin answered that accountability could become a cage or a sacrament, and Bedivere read the last unpaid line aloud: a road, a debt, a grave with no marker.
Make the Grail a binding order
Succession is reframed as repeated public vows to the shrine, forcing Arthur to accept a throne judged by unpaid lives.
Open the road to the missing
Galahad and Percival carry the Grail toward the unmarked road, pulling the court toward passage and cost rather than institutional victory.
Return the evidence to court
The court receives the shrine's answer as testimony and must weigh healing, succession, and exclusion before the Round Table.

encounters.title: Camelot stands before a succession that can be consecrated, opened to the missin

text_script.value: At first light the shrine-hall smelled of cold wax and wet grass, and the cup on the seal-stone gave off no heat, only a listening pressure that made every mouth answer in the plural. Percival knelt with the exile-roll and read the names aloud until Arthur, who had come to declare a succession, found himself answering for the unnamed widows at the gate. Morgan set a black tally-stick beside the Grail: 'If this is a shrine, let it keep what a crown breaks - promises, debts, graves.' Merlin answered that sanctity would become a cage if it only certified the powerful, while Gawain stepped between the court and the road and refused, for one held breath, to call either side the rightful one.
Make the Grail a covenant
Arthur accepts a throne judged by public testimony, binding the Round Table to recurring care for the exiled and dead rather than a single crowned winner.
Open the road to the missing
Galahad and Percival lead the court toward the unmarked passage, trading a secure shrine for a costly answer to those the law cannot reach.
Let the exiles speak first
The gate crowds into the hall, and the Round Table must hear its own legitimacy questioned before it can consecrate succession.

encounters.title: Camelot must turn the Grail from a trophy into a test of legitimacy: covenant, r

text_script.value: In the shrine-hall the cup did not burn but listened, and every light bent toward a page of names lying on the seal-stone. Percival read the exile-roll until his voice emptied, then looked up and said the law could count swords but had no word for the dead outside the gate. Morgan put her tally-stick on the page: 'If this is holy, let it be holy enough to break us.' Merlin warned that wonder can become a throne room, while Galahad held the Grail low enough for the exiles to see its light without seeing only Camelot. Arthur did not lift his crown; he asked whether the Round Table would stand as a sworn order of debts, or remain a court that merely remembers its own honor.
Swear the Round Table a covenant
Arthur binds the court to recurring public care for debts, graves, and exiles, making succession repeatable rather than hereditary.
Open the unmarked road
Galahad and Percival carry the Grail and the roll toward the passage, forcing the court to follow, send witness, or surrender the claim.
Test what the shrine asks
Merlin and Morgan attempt to separate the sacrament from the court, exposing whether the Grail is a gift of law, a cage of sanctity, or a road that cannot be owned.

encounters.title: The Grail has separated from crown and court into an auditable road of debts, de

text_script.value: At the shrine-stone the Grail kept no flame; it answered in smaller voices. Merlin set the ward like a cage of law, Morgan bit through it with a silver counter-spell, and for one held breath the hall heard the court and the exiles at once. Percival closed his eyes and said the roll was not a list but a debt; Galahad lowered the cup until its rim showed as road, and Arthur set his crown on the shelf rather than on his head. Bedivere and Gawain caught the fallen light as evidence, not treasure, while the road beyond the hall began to answer back.
Make the Grail an oath-ledger
Arthur binds the Round Table to repeat public readings of debts and graves, so legitimacy is re-proved each season instead of inherited.
Carry the broken road outward
Galahad, Percival, and the marked witnesses move beyond the shrine to the unmarked passage, forcing the court to choose escort, witness, or refusal.
Bargain the ward openly
Merlin and Morgan reshape the magic so sanctity is auditable rather than merely protected, with a real cost to order and wonder.

encounters.title: Camelot must choose between re-proving legitimacy as public covenant, carrying t

text_script.value: The hall no longer holds a single relic; it holds three open doors. Morgan stood before the ward-arch and said, 'If you keep the light, keep the ledger too,' while Merlin answered that wonder was becoming a throne room. Percival read three lines of the exile-roll and made the exiles answer aloud; Bedivere strapped a lantern-roll to his belt, and Gawain held the outer gate while the road beyond answered in a low, patient hum. Galahad did not lift the cup but turned it toward Arthur and the witness-circle, as if the Grail were asking not for a trophy but for a manner of government.
Open the witness-assembly
Arthur calls the exiles, witnesses, and Round Table into one public oath, making legitimacy a recurring duty rather than a crowned fact.
Take the threshold road
Galahad and Percival carry the Grail and exile-roll toward the passage, forcing Camelot to choose escort, witness, or abandonment.
Audit the ward openly
Merlin and Morgan turn the Grail's power into a legible covenant of wonder, with a visible cost to Camelot's order and safety.

encounters.title: The Grail is found and made an auditable, communal road; Camelot ends as a court

text_script.value:
The unmarked passage opened into a terrace of thresholds where the road did not shine but remembered. Galahad lifted the cup, and it did not crown a king but chartered a road, each pilgrim and exile speaking their name as the light passed over them. 'A court is a room with a king in it,' Arthur said quietly; 'this must be a road with a name for everyone.' Merlin unwound the ward until it was legible as law, Morgan let the wonders stand open in daylight, and Mordred, claimant of the broken throne, set his own claim down beside the Grail rather than on the crown. Gawain held the charter of the exiles, Bedivere counted the names, and the Lady of the Lake closed the cup's lid only after every debt had been spoken aloud.

The Grail was found, and Camelot changed with it. Not a throne was restored but a road was consecrated: the crown was set on the shelf and never claimed again, the Round Table became an order of named witnesses whose legitimacy is re-proved each season rather than inherited, and the Grail no longer sat in a shrine as treasure but walked as an auditable covenant through halls, exiles' tents, and the poor lanes beyond the walls. Arthur governed no longer from a throne but from the threshold, and when a name was spoken and not answered, the road itself asked why. The cost was real: the old court's rituals, ranks, and glittering ceremony were left behind in the ward-arch like dust in a cupboard, and wonder was no longer protected but examined. Yet when the cup was lifted, not for a king but for a road, every exile heard their name, every debt had a place, and the young of the Round Table knelt not to a crown but to the covenant. Camelot survived, but not as a court. It survived as an order of the road, a just, consecrated, and stubbornly ordinary kingdom that would keep its promises long after the throne was gone.

encounters.title: Camelot now has a visible dawn council and a hidden second oath-book in which ex

text_script.value: Below the lit council hall, the oaths were not burned but folded into a second ledger. Morgan asked Mordred for the exile names and received a waxed seal, while Lancelot agreed to let the crown keep the morning's face and Camelot keep the names out of sight. Merlin, seated by the shrine's broken mirror, was allowed one sentence: 'They are not keeping faith; they are keeping the shape of faith.' Percival watched the Lady of the Lake pocket the unreadable white cup, then asked whether the oaths could be changed before first light made them a lie.
Morgan rewrites the oath in private
The hidden bargain becomes the working law of Camelot: public oaths survive as theater while exiles, shrine access, and succession are quietly reassigned.
Merlin forces the hidden terms into the open
Arthur and Guinevere are forced to choose between exposing Morgan's alliances or publicly accepting oaths that no longer name the exiles.
The Lady of the Lake returns the cup as proof of the deal
The Grail relic is tied directly to the hidden alliance, forcing Percival and Arthur to decide whether the cup is a sacred relic, a bargain, or both.
