encounters.title: The claim is bound to Mordred's arm, the exiles are named at the gate, and Arthu

text_script.value: In the last lamp-light, Mordred took the wrapped claim from his coat and unwrapped it only enough to see the stitched edge, then bound it around his own forearm with a strip of linen while Gawain said, 'It was never a right to hold; it was a debt to see.' Lancelot answered that the road had been the only table that did not ask him to lie about wanting it, and Guinevere closed the exile rolls and asked Percival to name the first voice who had not been answered. Percival said the widows outside the gate asked for a word and for someone who would carry it, and Morgan touched the lamp once and said the thread would not know the road unless they agreed what it meant. Arthur did not lift the crown; he asked the table whether it was a place or a promise, and the court answered, for once, without ceremony.
Guinevere and Percival carry the word and the thread-lamp through the gate
The fellowship leaves the shrine and answers the exiles directly, but the lamp and the Grail cross a threshold where Camelot's law no longer fully holds.
Arthur asks Mordred to carry the bound claim as a named bearer
Mordred either enters the fellowship openly as a bearer and changes the table's meaning, or refuses and leaves it a closed memorial.
Arthur leaves the Cup unlit and witnesses swear by ordinary word
The fellowship is sealed by speech and witness rather than relic, keeping the Grail free but leaving no sacred oath to anchor it.

encounters.title: The court has made the exiles visible and the claim personal, with the Round Tab

text_script.value: The gate lanterns failed one by one, and Mordred did not step back from the wrapped claim; he showed it to the widows queued at the threshold and named each name as if it were his own debt. Gawain went around the bare Round Table and put his hands on the emptied seats until the wood sounded hollow, then said the table had always been a promise with no one to hold the other end. Morgan asked Merlin what the thread would do if no one stayed to keep it bright, and Merlin answered that a thread could be followed by one who refused to call it power. Arthur looked from the unlit Cup to the exiles' shadows and asked the court what it wanted to be when there was no longer a court: a throne, a promise, or a road.
Guinevere and Percival carry the lamp-thread beyond the gate
The fellowship answers the exiles directly, but the lamp and any Grail-bearing trust move into a country where Camelot's law and safety no longer guarantee them.
Arthur makes Mordred a named bearer of the claim
Mordred either enters the fellowship openly and turns the table into a living, costly practice, or refuses and leaves Camelot as a closed elegiac shrine.
Arthur swears the covenant over the unlit Cup
The fellowship is sealed by word, witness, and oath rather than relic, but loses the Grail as a visible anchor and must rely entirely on memory and mutual keeping.

encounters.title: The court is split between exile, claim, oath, and road, and every witness is no

text_script.value: Arthur sets the lamp on the bare table and says, 'Tell me what you will carry if this court no longer governs anyone.' Guinevere reads the widows' names until the flame leans toward the door, while Gawain lifts an empty seat and finds the dust line where a body used to lean. Mordred, his wrapped forearm steady, tells the court that he will not come back unless they ask him to; Lancelot says a table is only a promise when somebody refuses to sit alone at it; Morgan murmurs that the road can still be sung, but only if the songs are true. Merlin answers that Camelot may not return as a crown, yet it may return as a road with a name.
Carry the word beyond the threshold
Guinevere, Percival, and Bedivere leave with the lamp and the names, turning Camelot into a carried shrine rather than a fixed capital.
Arthur swears the covenant over the unlit Cup
The fellowship is sealed by speech and witness, freeing the Grail from power but leaving it outside any sacred oath.
Ask Mordred to carry the claim as named bearer
Mordred either accepts the debt and makes the road costly and real, or departs and leaves the Round Table as a closed elegy.

encounters.title: The court has named its debts and the lamp-thread is ready; the witnesses must n

text_script.value: The lamp thread hangs unlit above the bare table, and at the threshold Mordred stands wrapped against the cold, saying that if the court is done with law it is no longer done with its obligations. Guinevere reads the widows' names aloud until her voice stops shaking, and Arthur hears the court ask itself whether a promise kept in an empty hall is a keeping or only a mourning. Merlin says the Grail can be carried, but only by those who are willing to be ruined carrying it, while Morgan answers that ruin, kept honestly, may still be a form of law. Lancelot looks at the empty seats and says that no table has ever kept anyone warm unless someone refused to sit alone, and asks Arthur whether the court is willing to be that kind of ruin.
Walk the names and lamp to the exiles beyond the gate
The fellowship leaves Camelot as witnesses and keepers, binding itself to the exiles' survival but dissolving the court's public authority and the safety of its relics.
Arthur swears the covenant over the unlit Cup
The fellowship is sealed by speech, witness, and mutual keeping rather than relic, freeing the Grail from power but leaving Camelot as a memory-keeping place.
Ask Mordred to carry the claim into the ruin
Mordred either accepts the debt openly and turns the fellowship into a costly living practice, or refuses and leaves the Round Table as a closed elegiac shrine.

encounters.title: The court is at the point of deciding between sending the names beyond the gate,

text_script.value: The unlit lamp thread trembles above the bare table while the court tries to choose before the cold makes one choice the only one left. Guinevere, still folding the widows' names into a cloth, asks Mordred not for forgiveness but for a name: the name by which the ruin will answer if the road is kept. Lancelot sets his sword down between two empty seats and says that loyalty without a threshold is only weather, while Merlin answers that a threshold kept without love is a wall wearing manners. Beyond the arch, a small warm light moves along the road as if something tiny is being sent out to be found.
Send the names and lamp out with Percival and Bedivere
A small escort leaves Camelot carrying the names and lamp, turning the court into a portable shrine but separating it from the safety of its walls.
Arthur speaks the covenant over the unlit Cup
The fellowship is sealed by witnessed speech, freeing the Grail from office but leaving it unguarded, unarmed, and outside any sacred power.
Ask Mordred to carry the claim into the ruin
Mordred either accepts the debt openly and makes the road costly and real or refuses and closes the Round Table into a fixed elegy.

encounters.title: The court stands at the threshold with the names unfolded, Mordred waiting to he

text_script.value: Mordred remains just inside the broken arch rather than crossing the hall, and Arthur tells him that the table will not choose until every name has been heard in the room. Guinevere has unfolded the last cloth again; Lancelot presses a bare heel into the floor and says that an order spoken into an empty room is still an order, even if it can no longer be enforced. Gawain asks what the Round Table would do if no one were safe at it, and Percival answers that it would keep the road instead of the walls. Beyond the oaks, one small warm light is moving toward the hills, and Merlin says that whatever the court chooses will either travel with that light or admit that the light is all that remains.
Send Percival and Bedivere with the names and lamp
The fellowship becomes a traveling shrine for the exiles, but Camelot's relics and public authority are left unguarded behind the wall.
Arthur relights the Cup once and speaks the fellowship oath
The fellowship is sealed by one witnessed act of keeping rather than by office, leaving the Grail free of power but without a sanctuary.
Ask Mordred to carry the claim into the ruin
Mordred either accepts the debt openly and turns the table into a costly living practice, or refuses and freezes Camelot into a fixed elegiac shrine.

encounters.title: The covenant has been spoken once over an unlit Cup; the court now chooses betwe

text_script.value: Arthur has spoken the covenant once over the unlit Cup, and the words hold the hall without filling it; Guinevere folds the last cloth and tells Mordred that a name carried out into the dark is not lost, it is carried. Mordred stays within the broken arch and asks what the ruin would ask of him, and Arthur answers that it would ask him to answer first. Lancelot says that loyalty without a threshold is only weather, and Gawain says that a table meant nothing once a lamp could walk away from it. Beyond the gate the small light has gone still, and Merlin leans close to say that it is not leaving; it is waiting to be answered.
Send Percival, Bedivere, and Lancelot out with the lamp
The fellowship becomes a traveling shrine toward the exiles, but Camelot's relics and public authority stand unguarded behind the wall.
Keep the broken table as a public vigil
Camelot becomes a guarded elegy rather than a living road, and the court stays inside its walls with the names.
Ask Mordred to carry the claim into the ruin
Mordred either takes the debt openly and makes the road costly and real, or refuses and forces the court to choose without him.

encounters.title: The court stands at the threshold after the covenant is spoken, with the light b

text_script.value: Mordred stays at the threshold while Guinevere folds the last cloth and speaks the names of widows, exiles, and road-keepers aloud, until the hall no longer holds a courtier's certainty. Lancelot lays his sword across the empty chair but does not take it up, saying that a road cannot be promised to those who no longer have a way home; Arthur answers that the road is the oath, not the road itself. Merlin reports that the light beyond the gate has grown brighter without moving, and Morgan says that the old magic can keep it visible but cannot choose for those who must follow it. The gatekeeper has gone quiet, and the court leans toward the question of whether to answer the light or only remember it.
Arthur and companions go out to meet the light
The fellowship becomes a living road toward the exiles, but Camelot's relics and public authority fall silent behind the wall.
Keep the broken table and give it a new office
Camelot becomes a guarded elegy that witnesses the loss without sending anyone toward it.
Ask Mordred to carry the claim outward
If he accepts, the ruin gains a living bearer; if he refuses, the court must carry the claim itself and become more purely commemorative.

encounters.title: The court stands ready to choose between sending a guarded lamp beyond the gate,

text_script.value: Arthur sets the unlit Cup on the stump of a broken pillar and makes each companion name one lost person aloud before touching the relic; when Mordred asks what he should be, Gawain answers that a bearer is not a keeper but a witness who keeps the debt walkable. Merlin reports the light still brightening beyond the gate, while Morgan says the old magic can hold the shape of the road but cannot choose its walking. Mordred stands close enough to see his own reflection in the dark window and says, in a voice almost level, that if he carries the claim he will not carry it as a winner; he will carry it as a debt owed by every one of them. Lancelot, who has not sat down since the covenant was spoken, asks why a table should be mourned if it is still able to hold people.
Send Arthur, Lancelot, and Percival with the lamp to the boundary
The fellowship becomes a living road toward the exiles, while Camelot's relics and public authority remain open to the ruin.
Keep the broken table and define it as a standing covenant
Camelot becomes a guarded elegy that testifies to loss without sending the court beyond the wall.
Ask Mordred to carry the claim outward with one witness
The claim becomes concrete and costly, but if Mordred refuses or is lost, the remaining court must bear it alone.

encounters.title: The fellowship survives as a memorial covenant rather than a throne: Camelot kee

text_script.value:
By the last lamp the court did not arrange itself as a government; it arranged itself as a witness. Arthur set Guinevere's brooch on the broken edge of the table and let Lancelot, Gawain, Percival, Bedivere, Merlin and Morgan each say what the Round Table had meant when no office was watching, while Mordred stood outside the light and listened with the same attention he had once used for rule. When Arthur asked whether any of them would still be called by that name after the crown was gone, Guinevere answered that yes, if names were given away rather than kept, and Lancelot said the fellowship would survive only by learning to be smaller, slower and more honest than the court that had once governed by it. Merlin closed the gate lantern without naming it a king's law, Morgan bound the last road with memory instead of oath, and the Round Table became a place where the living could remember the dead without pretending the memory would feed them bread.

The Last Table is not a victory and is not a triumph over ruin. It is a choice to make love, duty, memory and mercy visible after the law of the throne has gone quiet. Arthur no longer holds a court, but he still holds a promise: that no name will be lost, no widow ignored, no exile unremembered, and no friend left to answer alone. Guinevere gives the names away instead of keeping them. Lancelot gives his divided loyalty to the living rather than the crown. Gawain, Percival, Bedivere, Merlin and Morgan turn discipline into care, and even Mordred is made to hear that bearing a claim is not the same as owning power. When the lights go down, Camelot is not restored; it is transformed into a table for the dead and a road for the living, where fellowship is the only law left, and its glory is measured not by what it governs but by how faithfully it remembers whoever must carry the light beyond it.

encounters.title: Camelot has begun rebuilding as law and commerce: a charter of contracts, stampe

text_script.value: At first bell the court of oaths had become a counting-house. Kay swept ledger-boards across the shrine table while Bedivere laid out iron tokens, each stamped with a name, and argued that an oath written on wax could be repaired by a witness, while an oath sworn on the road could not. Arthur watched the empty cup catch the dawn and asked whether a contract could hold where an army could not, and Kay answered that it would hold only where people were willing to be paid to keep it. Mordred listened with his jaw set, saying that a ledger was a chain with softer links, while Guinevere observed that a hostage was just friendship with an address.
Kay opens the covenant market at the shrine threshold
Traders, widows, and exiles enter under written terms, turning Camelot toward a durable merchant republic even as knightly glory fades.
Bedivere pledges named hostages between the factions
Arthur and Mordred exchange pledges of family and land, making war easier to deter and friendship visible and accountable.
Arthur leaves the road open beside the charter
The charter governs Camelot while the road remains a live question, keeping the Grail adventure from being closed by contract.

encounters.title: The charter is becoming a working town rather than a feast: outer parishes can p

text_script.value: At the second bell the market had crept off the shrine lawn and into the outer wall, where chalked lanes ran beside lantern-lit stalls and every wagon tongue carried a written name. Kay proposed a standing grain-and-toll pact: the outside parishes would keep the roads and harvest if Camelot kept their claims, their widows, and their debts visible instead of forgiven by legend. Mordred answered that a pact could outlast a knight but not a disappointed son, while Lancelot asked whether a written promise could survive him loving someone it could not fairly name; Guinevere suggested the contract should name the future rather than the feelingâ€”grain, labor, an apprenticeship, a protected exileâ€”and Arthur answered that the point of writing it down was that it could be audited when pride could not. Merlin watched the Grail road turn from an answer into a lane with a toll-keeper, and Gawain set his shield down against the ledger table, not as a surrender but as an entry in the ledger.
Kay binds the parishes to grain and labor
Camelot gains a real survival economy, but the outer towns must decide whether they are citizens in a republic or debtors dressed as citizens.
Bedivere makes hostage-claims public and revocable
Arthur, Mordred, and Lancelot exchange accountable promises that can be argued over, forcing private loyalty into the open.
Arthur opens the Grail lane as a toll-road
The road stays alive for oath, magic, and search, while its users must now accept that sacred passage may be taxed and shared.

encounters.title: The charter is now an argument about who may speak at the road: ratified parishe

text_script.value: At the third bell the toll-keeper had a brass ledger under his arm, while the parishes came in two loose parties: farmers with grain sacks, exiles carrying letters, and a few knights who still carried shields but no certainty. Mordred called the toll-road a leash with a sign saying free, and Merlin answered that the Grail lane had never asked for a temple so much as a door that could be argued at. Lancelot tried to put the name of the woman he could not fairly name into the charter and could not make the clerk accept it, so he opened a separate page headed not yet. Guinevere asked for the outer poor to speak before the oath-clerk, and Arthur agreed on one condition: every claim must survive its own hearing, including the ones that wound.
Kay ratifies the toll lane
The parishes enter the republic under written terms, but sacred passage must now be shared, taxed, and defended by ordinary people as well as knights.
Guinevere seats the exiles before the oath-clerk
Ordinary people get a public voice and a real chance to bind Camelot, forcing Arthur to choose between protecting the court and admitting the claimants.
Lancelot writes the not yet page into the charter
Private loyalty becomes a witnessed legal page, forcing Lancelot to decide whether love can be recorded without being spent.

encounters.title: The charter is now under frost pressure: grain credit, public exile-claims, Mord

text_script.value: At the fourth bell the frost found the market stalls first: chalked toll-marks faded on wet slate, and the parishes brought grain sacks that were heavier than their cheerfulness. Mordred said the republic would not be saved by generosity, only by a chain that could be cut when convenient, while Bedivere answered that chains could be audited and glories could not. Lancelot opened the not yet page and read only the clerk's wording aloudâ€”witnessed, not owedâ€”until Guinevere asked whether the court would accept a promise that could not be spent but could still be broken; Arthur said yes, if the breaker had to stand in the hearing too. Merlin touched the Grail lane with one finger and heard it hum like a road that had learned to keep its own toll.
Kay stakes the republic on frost-proof grain credit
The parishes gain a survival loan with public repayment, but Camelot now risks survival by becoming the ledger for people it cannot love easily.
Bedivere turns hostage-claims into revocable friendship
Arthur, Mordred, and Lancelot become auditors of one another, forcing private loyalty into evidence without making it an asset.
Lancelot speaks the not yet page before the court
The page becomes a witnessed claim rather than a debt, letting love enter the law while keeping it outside commerce.

encounters.title: Camelot now stands at the threshold of Merchant Peace: parishes are being conver

text_script.value: At the fifth bell the republic had stopped treating the frost as a weather problem and started treating it as a debt. Kay opened a waxed ledger at the road-hall and named each parish by the grain it owed, the toll it could pay, and the right it could refuse; Mordred answered that a peace written in arithmetic would wear the court like a chain, and Bedivere replied that chains could be inspected, locked, and traded, while glory could only break. Guinevere seated two exiles and a toll clerk beside the oath-clerk as witnesses, not as decorations, while Lancelot read only one line of the not yet page aloud and then asked for a market seal rather than an oath-ring. Merlin touched the Grail lane and heard it hum less like a relic than like a road that had learned to make promises survive winter, and Gawain said the watchmen must be allowed to say no without becoming traitors.
Kay seals the road-market
Parishes enter Camelot as audited traders with repayable rights, making survival more durable but turning sacred passage into a managed instrument.
Guinevere seats exiles as witnesses
Ordinary people become lawful witnesses with real standing, forcing the court to defend liberty by governing rather than by proclaiming it.
Arthur and Mordred make succession an office
The throne becomes a revocable office audited by all parties, weakening blood-legitimacy but giving Mordred a survivable future inside the republic.

encounters.title: The peace is now taking shape inside the toll-gate: the succession is moving fro

text_script.value: At the sixth bell the court met inside the toll-gate itself, where the ledger clerks had chalked the borders in chalk that could be erased by rain. Mordred stood before the gate and asked what would stop the office from becoming a new crown wearing a clerk's face, and Arthur answered that it would be audited every season by the same people it governed. Gawain's watchmen tested the gate by refusing a toll the clerks said was owed, and Guinevere seated a widow and her toll clerk beside Arthur as the first revocable auditors, not as decorations; Lancelot read one line aloud from the not yet page and then gave his seal instead of his ring. Merlin touched the Grail lane and heard it settle into a low, even hum, and Kay wrote the only word that had survived the winter in the ledger margin: enough.
Arthur accepts the office of Keeper rather than the crown
Succession becomes a revocable office audited by the governed, giving Mordred a future inside the republic while making Arthur answer for his role each season.
Gawain writes the watchmen's refusal into the charter
Law gains a right to say no, but order now depends on witnesses rather than a single throne, and every refusal becomes public and auditable.
Guinevere lets the widow test the charter before the court
The republic is judged by one ordinary household, forcing the court to defend survival as a right held by the governed rather than a favor granted by kings.

encounters.title: Camelot is now a working republic under frost and debt: the office is real but r

text_script.value: On the seventh morning the frost left chalk marks on the road but not on the bargains, and the court met around a ledger rather than a throne. Kay spread the pages and said, 'We are not buying a king; we are buying the right to be counted.' Mordred answered that a counting-house could still become a new crown with better bookkeeping, and Arthur said the office would close, not be crowned, if it could not survive the governed looking at it. Guinevere seated the widow's toll-clerk beside the seal, Lancelot asked for a market token rather than an oath-ring, and Bedivere proposed hostage-friendship: a named caravan, a winter grain promise, and a successor shown to both sides before either was forced to trust. Gawain's watchmen kept their keys visible and refused one debt in public, while Merlin touched the Grail lane and heard it answer the ledger with a low, patient hum.
Bedivere seals hostage-friendship pledges
Parishes trade caravan, grain, and successor promises instead of enemies, making survival stronger but turning trust into a watched market that can be bargained with.
Arthur turns succession into a rotating office
Arthur, Mordred, Gawain, and the widow-auditor share the duty of Keeper for fixed seasons, weakening blood legitimacy but forcing each claimant to prove survival before inheriting it.
Lancelot gives the caravan a market token
The sacred road becomes a traded instrument with portable tokens, letting the Merchant Peace survive winter but risking the Grail lane becoming another priced commodity.

encounters.title: The Merchant Peace is now tested by a missing caravan: the gate can close, open,

text_script.value: The winter bell found the court standing in the toll-gate arch while the caravan horn came thin from the north road. Kay had the ledger open but no grain chalk beneath it; Bedivere tapped the page and said the peace would have to be counted in bells, not boasts. Mordred asked what the Grail lane would feel if a wagon spent the night in its shadow, and Lancelot set the market token on the wood where Merlin could hear its low, unhurried answering note. Around the ledger, Arthur, Guinevere, Gawain and the widow's toll-clerk all leaned toward the same empty space where the caravan was supposed to be.
Bedivere replaces the hostage with named bell-watch surety
The court swaps human bondage for a public grain reserve, caravan letter, and nightly toll-watch, strengthening survival but making trust look like a watched tax.
Kay convenes toll-clerks and widow auditors to rule on closure
A jury of ordinary households can close or keep open the gate without waiting for the court, protecting survival but fragmenting law into local verdicts.
Lancelot limits the market token to the road, not the Grail lane
The shrine stays unpriced and eerily still while the caravan enters only under a conditional truce, trading glory for a durable but narrower peace.

encounters.title: The Merchant Peace has become a gate-jury calendar: caravan survival, shrine qui

text_script.value: The caravan horn did not return, and by midday the gate arch had become a tribunal: Bedivere read the toll-roll aloud, Gawain held two lanterns, and Merlin kept the Grail lane behind glass-cold quiet. Kay asked Mordred what he would give if succession were not a crown but a charge that could be refused, and Mordred answered with a road map, a winter grain promise, and one uncomfortable question: who would be left to deny him? Lancelot set the market token on the ledger's rim, where it answered no one; Guinevere had the widow's toll-clerk stand where the light showed his shoes; Arthur said the office would survive only if it could be argued with.
Kay asks the widow-toll-clerks to accept the gate
Ordinary auditors can admit or refuse the caravan and the Keeper office by sworn count, making survival fairer but harder to appeal.
Lancelot keeps the Grail lane sealed but sends grain past it
The shrine stays unpriced while the road moves, yielding a narrow peace that can hold one winter and break the next.
Arthur writes a refusal right into the Round Table
Even Arthur and Mordred can be denied the Keepership for failed deeds, strengthening law but making loyalty visibly conditional.

encounters.title: The Merchant Peace moves from gate rules to witnessed keepership: ordinary toll-

text_script.value: Midnight came down the north road as a thin second horn, and the court stopped pretending the missing caravan was absent. Kay set a writ beside the ledger and asked: 'Count what will still be food tomorrow.' Mordred answered from the threshold, 'Then I will pay the price of refusing,' while Arthur pressed his thumb to the empty line and said the refusal must be witnessed, not smuggled. Merlin kept the Grail lane under a glass-cold silence and added, 'It is quiet because it is being listened to,' and Guinevere brought the widow's toll-clerk into the light, where his shoes shone like two small promises.
Kay turns refusal into a public road writ
The caravan is admitted under sworn count, survival improves, but Camelot becomes visibly a court of contracts rather than a shrine-led realm.
Bedivere stakes silver and salt before the road moves
The grain reserve is proven and harder to seize, yet creditors gain standing at every feast and the peace starts to smell of purchase.
Lancelot lets Merlin open a witness window on the sealed lane
Sacred quiet survives, but custody becomes an inspectable magical office that ordinary households may believe and still distrust.

encounters.title: Winter survival is now a payable contract at the gate: Mordred offers grain and

text_script.value: Winter struck the north gate as a second horn, and the court was forced to turn ledgers into oaths. Kay held the winter count open on the table while Mordred leaned on the ledger's rim and offered his grain bond, his road map, and one unresolved word: who would stand to deny him. Lancelot set the market token beside the grain receipts and asked whether the office could be kept without the crown; Arthur answered that the office would survive only if it could be argued with. Merlin kept the Grail lane under its glass-cold silence and added, 'It is not guarded by silence; it is guarded by attention,' while Guinevere brought the widow toll-clerks to the light and let them hear that the seal was a bargain, not a miracle. Gawain took the toll-tolls into his hands and asked, quietly, what would happen if the count came out short.
Kay signs Mordred as Keeper under grain-and-road bond
The office is kept and the caravan moves, but Camelot is now hostage to one creditor's appetite and one winter's grain count.
Guinevere puts the widow toll-clerks in charge of the seal
The count becomes fairer and harder to seize, but the court loses its visible aristocratic legitimacy and must be trusted by those it governs.
Lancelot lets Merlin open one witnessed window on the Grail lane
Custody becomes inspectable and publicly believed, but the sacred silence is now a procedure that could be argued, misread, or broken by need.

encounters.title: The Merchant Peace advances from grain and tolls to named sureties: succession m

text_script.value: Dawn opened the north market like a door that had been persuaded to stay open. Kay laid the surety writ on the oak and asked, 'Name the kin who will answer for the table, and price him.' Lancelot answered, 'A hostage bought is only a promise with a heart in it,' while Mordred grinned from the threshold and said, 'Then pay with grain and call it friendship.' Arthur set his thumb on the empty succession line: 'If the table changes hands, the peace is only a tenant.' Merlin said the lane would still be listening, only now it would hear debts, and Guinevere brought the widow toll-clerks forward so the bargain could be read by hands that would live under it.
Kay signs the surety charter
Camelot becomes durable and legible, but the crown is now visibly collateral to a table of creditors and clerks rather than a shrine of final promises.
Bedivere pairs widow toll-clerks with Mordred's grain crews
Friendship becomes a working covenant, yet hostages-as-kin risk turning ordinary households into bargaining chips in the succession.
Lancelot asks Merlin to witness the debt without opening the lane
The Grail remains sealed while the peace is quietly consecrated by attention, but faith becomes hard to distinguish from administration.

encounters.title: The surety peace is under audit: the count is short by one row, the charter is p

text_script.value: The winter market came down the road with Mordred's caravan and found the granary count short by one row, and Kay made the ledger stand open before the whole hall. 'Count what is short,' Arthur said, 'and say what the peace is worth when the peace is short.' Gawain walked the stall-line with the toll-clerks while Mordred grinned at the shortfall: 'A missing sheaf is a chance to show who really owns the crown.' Lancelot answered that a short count could be a door if the house was honest, and Merlin said nothing at all, only held the Grail lane's glass-cold light at the back of the hall, waiting for the room to choose.
Bedivere opens the granary count to every eye
The shortfall becomes undeniable and the peace can be defended in the open, but whoever owns the missing row becomes the villain of the market and the chartered bargain is exposed to public blame.
Kay writes exile-work contracts for Mordred's crews
Ordinary households convert banishment into paid labor and the market stays open, but the exiles are now also creditors, and the peace carries a debt written in their own hands.
Lancelot asks Merlin to witness the market debt without opening the lane
The Grail holds its silence while the peace is quietly blessed by attention, but no ordinary hand can see what makes it real, and faith is harder to distinguish from administration.

encounters.title: The short row is marked in Mordred's own hand, the charter is public, the widow

text_script.value: The short row was still on the granary ledger, marked in Mordred's own hand, and the hall had stopped being a hall and become a counting room. Gawain walked the stall-line with the lantern until the marks blurred, then read them aloud while Kay held the charter open and would not let anyone read it first. Lancelot said, 'If the peace can be read by one eye, it can be argued by one hand,' and Mordred answered from the threshold that reading it aloud was a way of inviting the knives. Guinevere brought the widow toll-clerks up out of the work-gangs, and Merlin banked the Grail's light behind the room and said nothing, only kept it warm.
Kay binds the succession to household oaths
The crown becomes a legible instrument of ordinary households, durable and ugly in equal measure, and the Round Table is now a committee of creditors rather than a fellowship of oaths.
Gawain leads the recount under open lanterns
The short row is either exposed or forgiven in daylight, honesty is restored to the peace, but Mordred's crews and the crown's enemies are now publicly tied to the same ledger line.
Lancelot asks Merlin to witness the debt in silence
The peace is quietly blessed by a light no ordinary hand can see, but the hall no longer owns the proof of what makes the bargain real.

encounters.title: The charter is public but unresolved: the short row is marked, the widows wait a

text_script.value: In the second frost the charter lay between open palms, and the short row no longer looked like a ledger error but a question of whether the peace could outlive its own paper. Arthur said, 'If the ledger can be argued to death, then the crown is not sworn, only kept.' Mordred leaned over the mark and called the missing row a debt the crown could repay or a door it could open, while Guinevere watched the widow clerks decide whether fear or wages would steady their hands. Merlin kept the Grail lane banked behind the table and made the room feel less like proof than like a toll being weighed.
Kay swears widows and exiles onto a public surety roll
The peace becomes enforceable in daylight, but the crown is visibly a court of creditors and succession now depends on who can be vouched for.
Arthur and Merlin name the succession through witnesses
The Round Table becomes a court of judgment and oath rather than a market stall, durable in solemnity but harder to audit.
Bedivere and Gawain trade the short row for winter caravan shares
The merchant peace widens into useful grain, salt, and credit, yet the crown becomes a trader bound to the same debts it governs.

encounters.title: The peace now rides on a grain-and-salt caravan under a public charter, the shor

text_script.value: In the second frost the ledger had become a ledger of the living: grain chits stamped by Kay, salt contracts inked by Bedivere, and the short row still glowing faintly on the vellum like a held breath. Arthur set the charter on the table and asked Mordred plainly whether the row was a debt the crown owed or a key the crown could open, and Mordred answered that a caravan does not ask what the cargo is worth once it has already been loaded. Gawain wanted the short row read aloud to every widow in the hall, but Guinevere held up one hand and said that honesty had to be paid in the same coin it was borrowed — food, work, and a road out. Merlin kept the Grail lane banked and warm, and said only that the light did not care whether the crown was glorious or useful, only that it was not empty. The Lady of the Lake leaned over the table and asked whether the contracts could survive a winter without anyone being sworn to them.
Kay converts the short row into a grain-and-salt credit charter
The crown becomes an openly auditable debtor bound to its neighbors, ordinary households gain durable survival, and succession now depends on who can be vouched for at harvest.
Gawain trades the row for hostage-bonds with the Lake lords
The peace widens across the water and hostages become a language of friendship, but the crown's oath and the sacred witness no longer hold the crown together on their own.
Merlin seals succession inside the banked Grail light
The succession is blessed and durable, but no widow, exile, or Mordred crew can see, read, or audit what makes the bargain real.

encounters.title: The merchant peace now crosses the border as working grain, salt, credit, and gu

text_script.value: By the first plowed frost the road had become a contract in motion: wagons with grain sacks, salt cakes, stamped chits, and two guards paid in bread rather than banners. Arthur set the crowned ledger beside a short chain of coin that did not yet match the shrine's witness, and Kay said, 'If the crown feeds the road, the road remembers its face.' Mordred answered that feeding the road could also teach it to outrun the crown, while Gawain asked what should happen to a hostage who lived with the caravan and then fell in love with its ledger. Merlin banked the Grail lane low and pale behind the table, saying that the light could witness the peace without pretending it owned the people who lived in it. Guinevere leaned close to the widows' marks and asked whether the peace would remain honest if no one could sing about it afterward.
Kay binds succession to the caravan ledger
Succession becomes auditable and survives winter, but the throne becomes visibly a road office whose favorites are repaid by the same granaries that judge them.
Arthur and Gawain swear the succession across hostage and shrine
The bargain holds through public witness and hostage friendship, yet the oath now depends on both sides trusting a formula that can be examined and renegotiated.
Merlin banks the Grail lane as a neutral succession seal
The peace keeps sacred legitimacy inside the road without making magic the ledger, but the seal cannot be read by ordinary widows and exiles.

encounters.title: The merchant peace is about to cross the border under succession rules that can

text_script.value: At the border bell, Bedivere read the harvest chits aloud while Arthur held the succession seal in his palm; Mordred did not curse the ledger, but said that every yes made the crown answerable to wagons drawn by strangers. Gawain claimed that a hostage who wed a caravan family should have her share witnessed at the shrine, while Guinevere countered that love inside the road must not be converted into feudal debt. Merlin opened the banked Grail light just enough to show its shape, not its words, and the Lady of the Lake asked whether the crown could survive being legible.
Kay and Bedivere make succession an open caravan audit
The throne survives as a public road office with widows and exiles able to verify it, but favorites become hostages to granary judgments.
Gawain exchanges succession promise for Lake hostage friendship
The peace widens across the water and ordinary households gain durable contracts, yet the crown depends on strangers whose love can be tested and renegotiated.
Merlin seals succession inside the Grail witness
The crown is blessed and durable, but succession becomes sacred evidence that no widow, exile, or Mordred crew can fully read or challenge.

encounters.title: Succession now hangs between a readable widow-and-exile charter, a Lake hostage

text_script.value: At the dusk of the grain market, Kay laid the stamped succession seal beside a cracked ledger while Mordred asked what word would survive if the wagons left before the court did. Arthur said he would not bless a succession no widow could read, and the Lady of the Lake answered that no seal should outlive the households that made it. Gawain set a hostage-gift on the table, a bell, a loaf, and a written promise, while Guinevere asked whether love at the road's edge was a contract or a rescue; Merlin held the Grail light low enough to show its edge and not its words.
Kay fixes succession as a widow-and-exile charter
Succession survives by remaining readable to granaries, widows, and exiles, but the crown becomes dependent on ledgers and may alienate those exempt from their scrutiny.
Gawain makes Lake hostages part of the succession
The peace widens into durable friendship across the water, but Arthur must defend friends as a treaty while the Lake watches what the bargain can be asked to carry.
Merlin lets the Grail light witness without owning succession
The crown is blessed and durable, yet the sacred seal remains too far from ordinary life to serve as the only proof that the peace is real.

encounters.title: Succession now hinges on whether the crown can govern as a road — readable, coun

text_script.value: At first light over the grain road, Mordred's crew stood at the toll-house with their own tally-sticks, insisting the crown had never been theirs to bless. Kay slid a wooden counter-token across the table — not a seal, but a road-office oath — and Arthur demanded to know who would hold the crown when no oath could be sworn to it. Lancelot, who had kept his allegiance divided for years, spoke for the first time: if the road must be governed, then the crown should govern as a road, not as a court. Guinevere warned that love kept outside the bargain would come back with a claim of its own, and the Lady of the Lake answered that the Lake would witness any bargain it could still read aloud.
Kay swears the crown as a road-office oath
Succession survives as a public reckoning that favors no favorite, but the crown must answer to widows, exiles, and strangers at every toll.
Lancelot carries the dual oath between road and court
The crown gains a bridge across its divided loyalty, but Lancelot must carry the cost of a pledge that can never be fully discharged.
Merlin and the Lake seal the road-oath together
The peace becomes both sacred and legible, but the crown and the Lake are now bound in a permanent treaty neither side may loosen without grief.

encounters.title: The merchant peace is now taking shape as a readable road-treaty with tolls, gra

text_script.value: In the candlelit market-hall, Mordred unrolled his own tally-sticks and said the crown would not keep the roads honest unless it answered to them, not to ceremony. Kay wrote the first line of a public compact while Bedivere set granary sacks, toll-coins, and a cracked ledger beside it; Lancelot, pressed by Guinevere, chose to stand as bridge rather than judge. The Lady of the Lake set a smooth hostage-token on the table, while Merlin let the Grail light rest on the ink-line without blessing it into a spell.
Bedivere opens the market ledger to all parties
Succession becomes durable through counts, arrears, and shared tolls, but widows and exiles may find their dignity reduced to arithmetic.
Gawain and the Lake make hostages into granary pledges
The treaty widens across the water and endures through mutual protection, while every later quarrel becomes a hostage emergency.
Mordred receives the toll-office and a share of the peace
The crown survives as a working road-institution, but legitimacy splits into overlapping claims that no single seal can settle.

encounters.title: Succession now hangs on whether the crown may be sworn as a rotating road-office

text_script.value: In the rain-slick ledger hall, Bedivere laid the court's granary tally beside a second tally Mordred had written in his own hand, and read both aloud to Arthur: the crown's stores had shrunk while the road's tolls swelled. Mordred did not beg for the crown but offered to hold the toll-office open to every road, provided succession swore its first oath to the road, not to the bloodline. Kay answered that a crown sworn to strangers would have to swear the same to widows and exiles, and Lancelot set a hostage-token on the ledger — half granary, half oath — as a bridge neither side could break without the other paying. Guinevere watched the Lake-witness from across the table and asked whether the peace could be sworn to memory as well as to coin.
Kay swears the crown as a rotating road-office
Succession survives as a public office sworn to the road, but no single ruler can hold it — each succession becomes a fresh negotiation.
Bedivere reads the charter from the widows' tally outward
The peace becomes a charter of living obligations that binds the crown to the poor, but makes its authority a debt that must be continually repaid.
The Lake reads the oath aloud and returns the Grail light to the table
The peace is witnessed by the sacred and the civic at once, but the Grail is now bound to a succession that must be re-sworn before every change of office.

encounters.title: The merchant peace is sealed as a durable road-and-market coalition in which suc

text_script.value:
At dusk the sword rack stood empty while the market hall filled with sacks, toll-coins, tally-sticks, and quiet faces from roads that had not yet decided whether to forgive the court. Kay said the crown would no longer pay for honor with ruin, because honor had become a bad toll and a worse ledger. Bedivere laid contracts, bread allotments, grain shares, and arbitration slips beside Mordred's toll-office token, then struck the hostage-token from the table and replaced it with a public peace-bell. Lancelot kept his divided pledge visible but unclaimed, Merlin refused to bless the charter as a spell, Guinevere named the widows who would swear it aloud, and the Lady of the Lake answered that memory could witness what strength could no longer hold. Arthur did not proclaim a kingdom; he kept the peace honest enough to live in.

Camelot did not become cleaner, brighter, or more blessed; it became sturdier. Arthur held the crown as a custody of roads, granaries, widows, exiles, and disputed claims, while Kay turned pledges into contracts and Bedivere made the ledger public enough that no one could call a debt personal. Mordred kept the toll-office as a road-institution rather than a court weapon, Gawain and the Lady of the Lake made protection mutual without captive chains, Lancelot kept divided loyalty visible as a thread rather than a secret sword, Guinevere named the living obligations aloud, Merlin left the Grail to witness rather than command, and the ordinary people outside the hall learned that the peace could still be bought, questioned, amended, and defended. The glory did not disappear so much as change its shape: from a spectacle of defeated foes to a stubborn public covenant, less magnificent and more likely to outlive its kings.

encounters.title: Arthur has been released into absence; Camelot now faces preserve, replace, or r

text_script.value: At first light the throne room held only an empty seat, a Grail basin that had not so much as trembled, and a wind that smelled of cold water. Gawain pressed the crown toward Guinevere and asked what a crown was for if no one wore it, while Mordred answered that it was for the ones who refused to keep it - the widows, the exiles, the oathbreakers. Morgan, whose hand had drifted to the air where Arthur had stood, murmured that he had not been buried or taken but had been let go, and the court heard itself argue in a silence Arthur had already left.
Gawain swears the crown at the empty shrine
The crown is preserved as law and exile, binding the realm to Arthur's promise but risking a dead throne that protects only those already safe.
Percival and the Lady of the Lake carry the empty cup outward
The court splits into shrine-keepers and road-followers, and a new order is founded beyond the wall rather than on it.
The table is broken and the oath is refused
The crown, the cup, and the oath are all retired, leaving Camelot to be remade as witness, refuge, or ruin.

encounters.title: Camelot is visibly divided after Arthur's release into a shrine that guards his

text_script.value: The empty throne faced a chamber that had stopped pretending it was still a court. Merlin said the crown was not dead but unbalanced, Morgan warned that balance without a body might become only ritual, and Mordred told the room that a king who cannot be seen is a command no one can safely follow. Guinevere kept speaking to the vacant seat as if it were a witness, while Lancelot knelt with his oath unspoken and Percival lifted the Grail basin without setting it down. Bedivere watched the doors: one group would lock Arthur's absence into Camelot, another would carry it out beyond the walls, and the last would replace it with some small, named succession.
Gawain and Guinevere keep the empty throne visible
Camelot becomes a shrine of absence: exiles must petition for entry, oaths are preserved but narrow, and ordinary people outside the walls face exclusion unless they prove their need.
Percival and the Lady of the Lake carry the cup outward
The realm splits into a guarded Camelot and a moving order, forcing every oathholder to choose between the shrine and the road.
Mordred and Kay rewrite succession around wardens
The crown is replaced by a council of sworn keepers, ending one kingdom's myth and beginning a harder, more public experiment in governance.

encounters.title: With Arthur gone, Camelot must choose in three days how to hold his absence: a s

text_script.value: On the third morning the absence ripened into a deadline: Merlin said Arthur's ghost would not return, but the door of it would thin within three days unless the court chose how to hold it, and Morgan whispered that a house that decides nothing becomes Arthur's ghost. Percival stood with the Grail basin in both hands and said the cup had never been carried to a table that did not already know what it meant, so it could not be set down in a room that had not yet agreed who it served. Mordred and Kay laid the three proposed charters side by side on the empty throne as though reading rival wills, while Gawain kept reaching to touch the vacant crown and withdrawing his hand, and Lancelot looked from the shrine to the road and could not make his feet settle. Bedivere told them that outside the walls the widows and the road-exiles were not watching Camelot at all; they were already deciding whether this was a court, a shrine, or a rumor.
Gawain and Guinevere swear the threshold compact
The shrine and the road pledge to answer to each other, binding Camelot and the outward order to a shared duty but leaving neither fully free of the other.
Percival, the Lady of the Lake, and Lancelot carry the Grail outward
The cup leaves Camelot with Lancelot's divided loyalty at its center, and the court becomes a shrine that must remember the road or lose its meaning.
Mordred and Kay install sworn wardens over the shrine
Succession becomes public law of named keepers, ending the myth of the single king and obliging the shrine to answer to ordinary, contestable officials.

encounters.title: Camelot faces a three-way deadline to define Arthur's absence: preserve the empt

text_script.value: On the fourth day the silence had become an argument: Mordred spread two rival charters and asked who would be answerable if no king could be seen, while Kay counted the signatures that could be made public before the walls hardened against them. Morgan let a thin bright line flicker across the vacant seat and refused to say whether it was protection or an eviction, and Merlin answered that a ghost could be kept, carried, or dismissed, but never unchanged. Gawain kept reaching toward the crown and stopping himself; Guinevere answered the empty chair as though it were a petitioner; Percival and the Lady of the Lake held the Grail basin between the shrine and the road; Bedivere read the widows' and exiles' letters from outside, where the question was no longer what Camelot remembered but who it would feed tomorrow. Lancelot looked from the old throne to the cup and could not choose whether they were the same duty, and the chamber seemed to lean toward one of three definitions of Arthur's death.
Gawain and Guinevere bind shrine and road together
The shrine and the outward order swear reciprocal duties, keeping Arthur's absence visible but making every outside petitioner depend on Camelot's goodwill.
Percival, the Lady of the Lake, and Lancelot carry the Grail beyond the walls
The cup leaves the court and Camelot becomes a memorial that must justify why its people do not leave with it.
Mordred and Kay install sworn wardens over the shrine
Succession becomes a public office of named keepers rather than a myth of one king, forcing the shrine to answer to ordinary officials and contestable decisions.

encounters.title: Arthur's absence is now a live deadline: Camelot must choose between a reciproca

text_script.value: On the fifth day the empty seat stopped being a place and became a queue: outside the gates, Bedivere read two widows' petitions aloud while Percival held the Grail basin over a line of lamps, and Merlin told them the door of Arthur's absence was thinning into three possible contracts. Lancelot stood at the threshold and said that if the cup went out the court would become a grave with duties; Mordred answered that a grave with duties still feeds; Morgan let the air around the crown flicker like a coin caught in wind and refused to name the sound. Guinevere said the hard question was whether Arthur survived as shrine, as road, or as law, while Kay asked which of those could answer a knock at the gate before morning.
Gawain and Guinevere swear reciprocal shrine-road duties
The shrine and the road promise one another relief and judgment, but every widow, exile, and passer-through now has a standing claim on Camelot.
Percival, the Lady of the Lake, and Lancelot carry the Grail outward
The cup leaves the walls with Lancelot at its center, forcing the court to argue why it does not follow and making the outside world carry the same duty it no longer owns.
Mordred and Kay seat named wardens over the shrine
The throne is replaced by public, inspectable offices; the shrine answers to names and may be audited, expelled, or replaced if it fails the poor.

encounters.title: The court has reached a live split: audited shrine-road compact, cup carried to

text_script.value: On the sixth day the empty throne kept a slow toll while outside the wall the widows' line doubled and the exiles' cloaks pressed the road toward the gates. Galahad stood before the seal with an unmarked banner and asked Arthur, not anyone else, what he wanted done when he was only a pressure in the air; Morgan turned the pressure into a pale crown-shaped frost that guttered as if fed by wind. Merlin answered that a ghost could be kept, carried, or refused, but not obeyed; Lancelot laid his hand on the cup and said it would not be cleaner if it stayed home, while Mordred named the ordinary ledger and Kay read the names who would be answerable.
Gawain and Guinevere bind the shrine to public audit
The shrine-road compact becomes lawful and inspectable, but Camelot now answers to outside witnesses and may be judged by what it feeds rather than by what it remembers.
Percival, the Lady of the Lake, and Lancelot carry the Grail outward
The cup goes beyond the walls and pulls the widows, exiles, and Lancelot toward the road, forcing Camelot to decide whether it remains a refuge, a ruin, or a broken appointment.
Mordred and Kay seat audited wardens and seal the ghost outward
Succession becomes a named office answerable to oath and ledger, while Merlin and Morgan are forced to choose between sanctioning the seal or making the absence unmistakable.

encounters.title: Camelot is forced to turn Arthur's absence into either inspectable law, a portab

text_script.value: On the seventh day the gate stayed open and the empty throne stopped glowing; it hummed like a bell that had forgotten its note. Merlin set the ledger on the seat and asked who would be blamed if the cup fell; Morgan answered by brightening a hairline of frost at the throne's edge, and Galahad said the ghost could be testimony if he was not made into a monarch. Lancelot carried a wet banner toward the road, while Mordred, Kay, Bedivere, Percival, Guinevere, and Gawain argued whether the absence should be audited, carried, or left unbearable.
Merlin and Kay make Arthur's absence auditable
The court becomes a public instrument: oaths, stores, road debts, and succession are recorded, but survival may be governed by office instead of mercy.
Lancelot, Percival, and the Lady of the Lake take the road
The Grail and the widows' needs move beyond the walls, making the road the true court and forcing Camelot to defend a memory that no longer stays inside.
Galahad names the absence as witness, not crown
Arthur becomes a non-royal oath-light heard at the gate, leaving Camelot free to choose its next ruler without claiming the ghost as law.

encounters.title: Camelot is now divided into preserve, replace, or refuse responses to Arthur's a

text_script.value: On the eighth day the empty throne stopped looking like a vacancy and began to split the court, because one side heard it as testimony, another as an inheritance, and the road outside heard it as a debt. Mordred laid a ledger of heirs across the seat and named Kay, Bedivere, Galahad, and Percival; Galahad answered that an heir could be charged with the absence without claiming Arthur's name. Lancelot pressed a wet cloth to the cold brass and said a ghost should not be patched together with his own longing, while Morgan drew a pale frost-crown that would not shine unless someone admitted it was Arthur's. Merlin, Guinevere, Gawain, the Lady of the Lake, and Bedivere watched the widows' cloaks gather at the gate as though Camelot had already begun to choose what its ghost was for.
Gawain and Guinevere make the absence a public witness
Arthur's legacy survives as an inspectable office of duty rather than a crown, forcing every officer to answer for what the ghost is used for.
Mordred and Kay seat a named warden of succession
Succession becomes ledger and oath under a successor, but Arthur is replaced by an office that may become more powerful than mercy.
Lancelot, Percival, and the Lady of the Lake carry the absence beyond the walls
The Grail, the widows, and the road leave Camelot to decide whether memory can live outside a throne or collapses with it.

encounters.title: Camelot must now choose between a public succession office, a road carrying the

text_script.value: At noon the court stopped arguing in words and began arguing in consequences. Mordred opened the succession book and named Kay as ward, while Gawain swore before it that the absence had to remain testimony rather than treasure. Lancelot and Percival carried the Grail toward the gate, Morgan set a pale frost-crown where Arthur had stood and asked who would own the name, and Galahad placed a small lamp on the empty seat, daring Camelot to choose whether the light was for duty, warning, or escape. Guinevere asked where the widows would sleep if the court chose an office over the road, and Merlin, Bedivere, and the Lady of the Lake stood at the seams of the answer.
Merlin and Kay bind succession to public service
Succession becomes an auditable office of care, but survival may depend on forms more than mercy.
Lancelot, Percival, and the Lady of the Lake carry the witness outward
The Grail, the widows, and the absence move beyond the walls, forcing Camelot to defend a memory that is no longer only inside the gate.
Galahad and Morgan refuse the crown and leave the absence as warning
Arthur is neither monarch nor office but a shared light that can guide, shame, or haunt whichever ruler survives.

encounters.title: The court is now forced to choose between binding Arthur's absence to a sworn pu

text_script.value: At dusk the lamp on the empty seat would not stay lit; it leaned toward the door, as if the absence itself had begun to move. Mordred slammed the succession ledger onto the brass and declared that an office with no owner was a door left open, while Galahad answered that the office was owned by everyone who owed it a debt. Lancelot lifted the frost-crown and found it cold, hollow, and unmistakably Arthur's, and Morgan touched the gate stones and said the widows could not be promised a chair, only a place to sleep. Guinevere asked what would happen if the ghost was neither kept nor carried off, and Merlin looked toward the hills where the road to the Grail still ran pale in the first dark.
Merlin and Guinevere bind the ghost to a sworn office of witness
Succession becomes a publicly auditable duty under the court's own rules, but the office begins to crowd out mercy and the road.
Lancelot, Percival, and the Lady of the Lake take the lamp, the Grail, and the widows toward the hills
Camelot faces a real exodus, and the court must choose to follow, bar the gates, or watch the ghost leave the kingdom.
Morgan and Galahad leave the absence uncrowned and unbound
The court becomes a shared warning rather than a throne, but Arthur's name is no one's oath and Mordred may exploit the void.

encounters.title: The court now faces an open split: bind Arthur's absence into an oath-bound offi

text_script.value: By the third bell the court had split along old lines. Mordred set the succession ledger on the throne and spoke of an heir before dawn, while Lancelot answered that an heir without a king would inherit only a form. Morgan raised one pale hand and said the ghost was listening, not obeying, and Gawain drew the council's oath-ring toward himself and asked which of them had sworn to the road, the office, or the warning. Guinevere brought the widows' coats into the hall and let the sound of them brush the marble carry the argument louder than any speech.
Merlin and Kay seal the office with a public oath
The succession is formally bound and auditable, but the oath crowds out mercy and makes the office feel less like Arthur's ghost than a new gatekeeper.
Lancelot, Percival, and the Lady of the Lake take the widows beyond the gate
Camelot loosens its grip on the Grail and the widows, forcing the remaining council to choose whether to follow, guard, or abandon the road.
Morgan and Galahad refuse the crown and leave Arthur's name unclaimed
The court becomes a shared warning rather than a throne, but the void left by Arthur invites Mordred and other rivals to press their own claims.

encounters.title: The council is now choosing among an auditable witness-office for Arthur's ghost

text_script.value: By the fourth bell the oath-ring had stopped answering when any hand hovered above it, so Kay read the succession ledger aloud while the empty throne watched with no heat in it. Merlin held the frost-crown upside down and asked whether Arthur had left a crown to be worn, a question to be answered, or a warning to be carried, and Lancelot set the Grail close enough that the dark around it grew thinner. Morgan touched the gate stones and said the road was not a leaving but a bargain, while Mordred answered that bargains unnamed are just other ways to keep power; Guinevere, looking at the widows' coats still lying by the threshold, pressed the hard question: what would the court be worth if it could not tell a frightened household where its safety lived?
Merlin, Kay, and Bedivere swear the ghost as an auditable office of witness
The realm gains a public succession rule, but the ghost becomes a procedure and must be defended against being turned into another crown.
Lancelot, Percival, and the Lady of the Lake carry the lamp, the Grail, and the widows past the gate
The remaining court must either follow with law and bread, bar the gates as a fortress of memory, or watch the Grail and the widows leave the kingdom.
Morgan and Galahad keep Arthur's name uncrowned and unclaimed
The court becomes a standing warning rather than a throne, but Mordred and lesser rivals may argue that an unnamed ghost is an open claim.

encounters.title: The court has split into witness-office loyalists and road-carrying exiles, with

text_script.value: At the fourth bell the hall had split into two weathers: the sworn office kept its lamps lit, and the gate stood open for the widows who had gone with Lancelot. Merlin said the ghost was not dead but listening, and when he asked it one question, the lamps burned lower and answered with nothing. Morgan touched the empty throne and said a refusal could also be a claim, while Mordred answered that an unseen claimant was the oldest claim there was, and Gawain stood between the ledger and the open gate and asked which of them would carry the other side when the light failed. Guinevere brought the widows' coats back from the threshold and set them on the throne, saying the ghost had already left one thing in the world and they owed it a place to stand.
Merlin and Bedivere force the ghost to answer one question before dawn
The ghost either speaks once, confirming or breaking the office, or refuses again and turns the silence into a public claim that can no longer be audited away.
Lancelot, Percival, and the Lady of the Lake return with the widows and demand a seat in the council
The council must either admit the exiles into the succession question, or bar the road and leave the widows dependent on outside lords and oaths.
Mordred names himself guardian of the ghost and demands the ledger be read aloud
The legitimacy dispute turns on whether an unseen claimant may bind ordinary lives, and the office-keepers and road-carriers are pushed into open alliance or open break.

encounters.title: The court is split among a forced answer from the ghost, an open seat for the wi

text_script.value: Dawn found the council standing around a table where the ledger lay open but unread, its ink gone faint as if the ghost had been reading over their shoulders. Lancelot came through the gate with Percival, the Lady of the Lake, and three widows carrying folded coats, and set bread and water at the foot of the throne instead of at the council's elbow. Mordred said, 'A seal on a silence is still a claim,' and Merlin answered, 'Then let the silence choose what kind of seal it wants.' Morgan looked at the road and asked whether a kingdom survived by being entered, refused, or left standing empty.
Merlin and Morgan ask the ghost to name one living duty: oath, heir, or warning
If the ghost answers, Camelot gains a single testable rule but risks turning the empty throne into a scripted oracle; if it refuses, the silence becomes a public weapon in the succession fight.
Lancelot and the Lady seat the widows at the Round Table or at the threshold
Admitting them makes Camelot smaller but more honest, while refusing them forces the court to choose between barring the gate and carrying the widows beyond the kingdom.
Mordred reads the ledger aloud and declares silence a valid office
The office-keepers lose the certainty that an answer is needed, while the road-carriers gain a demand that no rule may be imposed on people who cannot vote, hold land, or speak.

encounters.title: Camelot has carried Arthur's empty throne to the road as a test of who will guar

text_script.value: Before first bell the council carried the empty throne out of the hall and set it at the top of the road where the widows had been left, and for a moment the whole court heard the wind move through the Grail cloth like a breath that had not been given back. Mordred said an empty throne was not a failure but a door, and asked who was willing to keep it open; Gawain answered that he would carry the threshold only if the threshold did not become a rule; Merlin asked whether the ghost, if it ever spoke, would be listened to as king, witness, or warning; Morgan answered that a kingdom feeds people who cannot enter the room, and Lancelot, without taking off his cloak, said the room would be made smaller until it could feed them. The widows stood behind the throne with their coats held flat against their bodies, and the Grail did not answer any of them.
Gawain keeps the throne at the threshold and opens a caretaker oath
The office gains a visible duty but must swear not to make the ghost an unverifiable god, forcing every successor to answer to widows and exiles before oath.
Merlin and Bedivere make the ghost answer one public question
A spoken answer or refusal turns the empty throne from symbol into a legal act, sharpening the succession fight without deciding who may sit.
Lancelot seats the widows as first witnesses at the Round Table
The court either accepts the road-carriers as rulers of the threshold or bar them and make the empty throne a claim held only by those with keys.

encounters.title: The empty throne stands on the road threshold with the Grail cloth over it, the

text_script.value: At first light the throne did not move; it seemed to gather the silence around it, and the road seemed to lean toward it like a hound. Merlin laid the Grail cloth across the empty seat and asked what it wanted kept, carried, or refused; Mordred answered that an empty office, sworn and sealed, was itself a kingdom. Lancelot set the widows' coats beneath the cloth so the relic could not be mistaken for a trophy, while Morgan said that oaths spoken in public must still survive being misunderstood. Gawain cut the seal-string with his knife and left both halves open, and the ghost remained nowhere in the sound of wind.
Gawain names a caretaker oath answered to the widows before the court
Camelot gains a visible duty but must police whether the caretaker is protecting the threshold or quietly becoming the new king.
Bedivere and Galahad demand one public answer or refusal from the ghost
The empty throne becomes either a testable legal act or an unanswerable refusal, sharpening the succession struggle.
Lady of the Lake divides fixed rights between inside and outside the gate
Exiles and widows gain real access to bread, shelter, and judgment, but the Round Table becomes smaller and more visibly provisional.

encounters.title: The empty throne still stands on the road, the widows wait with bread-bowls, and

text_script.value: At first frost the empty throne kept the road like a held breath, while the widows lined the lane with bread-bowls too small for the crowd. Mordred called the threshold an empty kingdom and asked who would feed it; Lancelot said the answer was whoever was forced to leave the room to find out; Merlin held a candle beside the Grail cloth and waited for it to burn toward the threshold, and Morgan countered that a claim visible from outside was not a claim stronger than a claim carried home. Bedivere noticed one golden thread detach from the cloth and crawl toward the gate, slow as frost, and Gawain laughed once as if the laugh might break the silence before it broke the court.
Gawain makes every heir swear to the widows before the court
Camelot gains a public duty and a hard test: anyone who accepts must answer to bread, shelter, and judgment before they may touch the Round Table.
Merlin and Bedivere read the moving thread as the ghost's first non-verbal reply
The empty office is recast from symbol into a testable relic, forcing the court to decide whether a sign is permission, warning, or evidence of a claim being made by something other than Arthur.
Morgan divides the Round Table into feeding stewards and legal watchers
The court loses its single ceremonial center but gains separate rooms for hunger, law, and magic, making succession look less like coronation and more like civil engineering.

encounters.title: The threshold is split into feeding stewards and legal watchers, the golden thre

text_script.value: The first frost did not quiet the threshold; it divided it into a bread-line on the left and a counting-house on the right, with the golden thread still crawling from the cloth toward the gate. Mordred called the split a provisional kingship, Guinevere answered that provisional meant hungry, and Lancelot told both that a relic fed by crowds was no longer a relic but a debt. Merlin touched the thread and felt it remember not blood but the weight of a bowl set down in a dark room; Morgan said that was precisely the memory a succession would need, or ruin. Bedivere slid Arthur's seal beside the road rather than above it, and Percival answered that if the seal refused to sit on a head, then it might have to guard the road's first guest.
Percival seats the seal beside the road as first-guest guardian
The Round Table becomes a doorway: whoever holds the seal must answer hunger, exile, and judgment before any claim is crowned.
Merlin and Morgan make the golden thread an audit of debts
The court turns the ghost's sign into ledger entries, letting widows, exiles, and claimants see exactly what Arthur is owed before he is asked to speak again.
Gawain opens the gate and refuses a successor
Camelot stops choosing a king and instead declares itself a ruined republic, leaving Mordred, Lancelot, and Morgan to fight over the terms of survival.

encounters.title: Camelot is splitting into three live responses to Arthur's absence: preserve the

text_script.value: On the eve of judgment the widows carried their bread-bowls up the hall and did not wait to be named; Mordred answered that a ghost could not keep a hearth, while Guinevere said a throne that ignored the hearth was already dead. Lancelot told Merlin to preserve Arthur as a test, not a relic, and Morgan asked what would happen to the parts of the Round Table that refused to become a coronation. Percival set Arthur's seal at the threshold so the first traveler would have to name need and oath before he could claim the road, and the golden thread paused above the gate as if listening for the answer.
Lancelot and Gawain guard Arthur's seal as a civic test
The Round Table becomes a law-court of promises, forcing claimants to answer hunger and exile before any crown may be spoken.
Mordred and Morgan rebuild the Round Table around feeding stewards
The throne is replaced by practical offices of bread, law, and magic, making survival possible but weakening Arthur's claim as king.
Percival declares the gate closed to successors until the seal can be answered
Camelot becomes a ruined sanctuary in waiting: no king is crowned, and factions must argue over who may enter, feed, or judge.

encounters.title: The threshold is now a contested jurisdiction: Arthur's seal waits at the edge o

text_script.value: By the second bell the golden thread had stopped shining and begun to weigh, a fine filament across the threshold like a rope held between two promises. Merlin said Arthur was not gone but refused to carry his own weight anymore, and Guinevere answered that refusal was not an office. Mordred spread bread, oath-stones, and law-books on the stone ledge; Bedivere set Arthur's seal at the edge of the crowd rather than above them; and the Lady of the Lake leaned close to the thread and said it was remembering the room where Arthur was last given something to carry. Percival lifted one hand to ask whether the ghost wanted to be kept, replaced, or allowed to leave the court altogether.
Galahad and Kay preserve the ghost as a public test of office
Claimants must state what they owe the dead king before the Round Table may meet, making Arthur a civic burden rather than a decorative crown.
Mordred and Morgan replace the crown with an office of bread, law, and threshold-watch
The realm gains working offices and survival, but the Round Table becomes less a sacred fellowship than a governing mechanism under suspicion.
Lady of the Lake and Percival refuse the ghost a throne and send the seal to the first traveler
Camelot turns outward from Arthur's absence, staking its future on hospitality and judgment rather than on succession.

encounters.title: Camelot now faces a practical schism: preserve Arthur's absence as a civic test,

text_script.value: At first bell the empty throne gave off no light, only a cold draft that bent the candles toward the gate. Merlin said the ghost was not dead and was not present; it was simply no longer obliged to answer questions. Mordred laid out bread, oath-stones, and unpaid debts as if office were a ledger that could feed a city, while Lancelot pushed Arthur's seal toward the threshold and said a claim without a debt was only a louder rumor. Percival read the crack in the seal as a request, not a verdict, and the widows waited in the aisle with their small hunger showing.
Lancelot and Gawain make the Round Table answer needs before crowns
The Round Table becomes a public ledger of hunger, exile, and oath, but the crown is suspended until those debts are answered.
Mordred and Morgan replace the ghost with bread, law, and threshold-watch
Camelot gains working offices and survival, though Arthur's absence is converted into a regulated system rather than a remembered kingship.
Lady of the Lake and Percival give the seal to the first true-need traveler
Camelot turns outward from succession and becomes a judgment-and-hospitality threshold that can admit the poor but risks losing its own court.

encounters.title: Camelot is split into ledger, threshold, and road camps, with Arthur's ghost now

text_script.value: By second bell the ghost had stopped being an absence and become a bargaining table: the seal's two cracks had stopped shining and begun to weigh, and the three camps of Camelot — ledger, threshold, road — were negotiating in public. Gawain said an oath owed to a ghost was not the same as an oath owed to the living, and Guinevere answered that the living had a long habit of mistaking the two, which was precisely the problem. Mordred laid three sealed coffers on the stone ledge: one for widows, one for exiles, one for the seal itself, and asked which would be opened first. The widows in the aisle made no answer, only looked at the cracks, as if waiting to learn whether the dead cared about their hunger.
Galahad and Kay make the ghost answerable: every office must swear to it
The Round Table survives as a test of office, but any oath that cannot feed or shelter the living collapses in open session.
Mordred and Morgan open the widows' coffer and charter the threshold-watch
The realm gains working offices and survival under a roof-rule, but the Round Table becomes a regulated charter rather than a sacred fellowship.
Lady of the Lake and Percival hand the seal to the first true-need traveler
Camelot turns outward and may leave its court behind, and Arthur's ghost itself travels with a stranger.
